D 0094 Half Day Format And Repeat Engagement Model

D-0094 — Half-day format, and how repeat revenue actually works

1. Format — decided by Hunter, 2026-08-09

The two products are a one-hour Introduction and a half-day Foundations Session. The 3-hour framing is retired as the flagship's name and shape.

Hunter, directly: "I think maybe with a one hour and a half day. I think the half day gives us more time. There'll be breaks in the day, which means we can charge more... we may only do three hours of actual work, but we go from, like, nine to one."

Working shape: roughly 9:00–13:00 elapsed, with approximately three hours of actual content and a substantial break (morning tea) inside it. The exact split is a delivery detail, not a framework decision.

Why this does not contradict D-0093's evidence finding

D-0093 concluded, from the strongest available evidence, that adding more sessions or more teaching content is not supported as a way to improve outcomes. This decision does not do that. The intervention is unchanged — still approximately three hours of content. What changes is the container around it: elapsed time, breaks, and how it is sold. That is a delivery and commercial decision, not a claim about efficacy, and it should never be presented to a buyer as though the longer day itself produces better outcomes.

Three things that independently support it

  1. The Committee already recommended exactly this. 04-product-pricing.md records the 20 July Committee session finding the ~$1,800 price too low and recommending repositioning toward $3,000–$5,000 for a longer, half-day-style format. Hunter's instinct here converges with a recommendation already on record, made independently and before this conversation.
  2. A half-day is a unit buyers recognise and price — but the benchmark partly cuts the other way, and that must be said. 05-commercial-and-buyer-pathway-model.md records $500–$2,000 per half-day (entry tier) and $2,000–$7,500 per workshop (mid tier). Corrected after independent review: an earlier draft of this record called these "verified benchmarks." They are not. The source file marks them unknown, vendor-published, single-sourced, with an explicit instruction that "none of it should be used in a funding application or board paper without independent confirmation." Worse, read honestly: the entry-tier half-day range tops out at $2,000 — below the $3,000 MFC would charge. Only the mid tier reaches $3,000, and it is priced per workshop, a different unit. The real support for a half-day here is that it is a recognised commercial unit, not that the benchmark validates MFC's price point. It doesn't.
  3. Breaks are a genuine participant benefit, not just packaging. A room that has eaten and moved is a better room. This is an honest quality improvement — it just isn't an outcomes claim.

What this changes downstream — and the objection that has to be answered

The existing pricing model's 3-hour worked example (base coverage fee + per-participant, capped at 20) carries over structurally, but every facilitator-time figure in it needs recalculating — delivery hours rise, and the current model's 6.5-hour estimate was built on a 3-hour session. Not done here; flagged for the pricing update.

The real value-for-money objection, named rather than avoided (added after independent review). "Same content, longer day, higher price" invites a buyer to see padding. Two things make that objection sharper than it first looks:

  • MFC's own cost rises too — more facilitator hours per session — so "we can charge more" is not free margin. How much of the increase is cost recovery versus genuine repricing is unquantified until the pricing model is redone.
  • The buyer's cost rises faster than the fee does. Twenty staff released for a half-day is far more expensive to an organisation than twenty staff released for three hours — the fee increase is the smaller part of what they are being asked to absorb.

The honest answer to give a buyer is not "it's longer so it costs more." It is that a half-day with proper breaks is a better-designed day for the people in it, and that MFC is pricing a recognised commercial unit rather than an awkward three-hour block. What must not be claimed is that the longer day produces better outcomes — D-0093 establishes there is no evidence for that, and this is the most likely place for that overclaim to slip in.

2. The repeat-engagement question — the finding that reframes it

Hunter's worry, repeatedly: MFC gets pigeonholed into one transaction per buyer, with no way back in, no repeat revenue, no "come back next year."

MFC's binding constraint is demand, not delivery capacity — but the reasoning has to be the right one.

Corrected twice. An earlier draft argued this from a Year 1 planning assumption of 5–11 engagements (04-product-pricing.md) against a much higher theoretical delivery capacity. An independent review found that circular — a planning figure is not observed demand. Hunter then set the figure aside entirely, 2026-08-09: it originated as Jake's early estimate, not a founder decision or a tested constraint — "I want us to forget those initial claims." No planning-volume figure should be treated as a limit anywhere in this record or downstream of it.

The non-circular basis, which is stronger anyway: MFC has delivered zero pilots, has zero paying buyers to date, and its own commercial research marks the workplace purchasing pathway as unknown (05-commercial-and-buyer-pathway-model.md) — nobody has established how these buyers actually buy, or what triggers the purchase. That is a demand-side unknown of the most fundamental kind, and it exists regardless of what any planning figure says.

Why the reframe still matters: if finding and converting a buyer is the expensive, unproven part, then repeat engagement is not primarily about filling spare delivery capacity — it is about making each hard-won buyer relationship worth more. That is the lens the options below are judged against.

3. Three ways to earn repeat revenue, ranked

Option A — Successive cohorts within the same organisation RECOMMENDED, available now

An organisation with 120 staff needs six half-day sessions at 20 participants each. One buyer relationship, six engagements, sold once.

  • No efficacy claim required — it is the same product delivered to different people, and nothing about it depends on D-0093's rejected booster premise. Corrected after independent review: an earlier draft said "evidence claims required: none," which was too clean. Rebooking still requires the organisation to believe session one worked — and MFC's only outcome signal is a follow-up at day 21–28, which arrives after a rebooking conversation would realistically happen. Selling all six cohorts upfront avoids that timing problem but invites heavier procurement scrutiny, which lands on exactly the evidence MFC does not yet have. There is no version of this that is genuinely evidence-free.
  • Design work required: none. It exists today.
  • Commercially natural: start with one team or the leadership group, expand across the organisation. Ordinary land-and-expand, the standard way small providers grow inside large accounts.
  • Honest limit 1 — it defers the problem rather than solving it. Six cohorts exhausts a 120-person organisation. Then the pigeonhole returns, just later. This buys time and revenue; it is not the permanent answer to Hunter's worry, and should not be sold internally as one.
  • ~~Honest limit 2 — concentration risk~~ — WITHDRAWN, 2026-08-09. This recommendation was wrong, and Hunter caught it. An earlier version of this record recommended capping delivery at two to three cohorts per buyer to avoid concentrating revenue and evidence in one organisation.

Why it was wrong — it contradicts this record's own central finding. §2 establishes that MFC's binding constraint is demand, not delivery capacity. Capping how much you sell to a willing buyer is a supply-side restriction, which only makes sense when supply is the scarce thing. It isn't. Hunter, directly: "if we did six with them... we don't lose money for that, we gain money... if an organization's like, we want you to attend with ten teams, we'd never say no." Correct. The cap would have meant declining revenue with no alternative buyer to redirect it to.

The "founding-cohort slots" framing that supported it is also withdrawn. It rested on the 5–11 engagements figure, which Hunter has identified as Jake's early planning estimate rather than a decided constraint, and has directed be set aside: "I want us to forget those initial claims." Treating an estimate as a scarcity limit was the error underneath the error.

What is actually true, and it points the opposite way: multiple cohorts inside one organisation is the best case-study condition MFC could have for the thing it most needs to evidence. D-0090/D-0091's environment and shared-norm work can only show up where enough people in the same organisation have been through the session — a single cohort of 20 in a 500-person company cannot demonstrate a norm shift; six cohorts might. Six sessions in one organisation is a strategic asset for the evidence base, not a risk to it. reasoning, not evidence — no MFC data exists either way yet.

Residual point, kept honestly and much smaller than the original claim: case studies across several sectors are eventually more persuasive to funders than several in one. That is an argument to also pursue other buyers, never an argument to refuse a willing one. - Honest limit 3 — organisation size. A 25-person business is one session and done. Option A does nothing for what may be a large share of MFC's realistic early market.

Option B — Extended Pilot Partnership, correctly positioned DESIGN IT, CAREFULLY

Already named and priced in 04-product-pricing.md (3–4 months, structured check-ins, up to −35% discount for full participation), explicitly flagged there as "the actual programme content is not designed yet."

  • What it legitimately is: measurement and implementation support. The organisation gets real data about its own people; the shared commitment from the session stays visible in normal work rhythms. MFC gets the longitudinal evidence it currently has none of.
  • What it must never be sold as: a booster that improves outcomes. D-0093 establishes that claim is contradicted by the strongest available evidence. This is a K-08 claims boundary, and it is the single easiest place in this whole model to overclaim by accident.
  • Low facilitator burden — reminders, a short review conversation — so it does not consume the delivery capacity Option A needs.
  • Honest risk, named: structured check-ins can quietly become de facto booster sessions, at which point the claim boundary is breached in practice even if the brochure is careful. Whatever gets designed needs an explicit line on what these check-ins are and are not.

Option C — A genuinely deeper second product LATER, NOT NOW

K-07's staged teaching arc already defines Stage 3 "Deepening" content that MFC does not currently sell at all: the seven deep skills, the full Radar (My moments / Our moments), the evidence layer.

  • This is real additional content, not a repetition of the first session — which is precisely what makes it an honest answer to "come back next year" where a booster is not. The claim is "this is more, for people who want more," not "this makes the first session work better."
  • Already designed at framework level, not invented here.
  • Why not now: no pilot has run, D-0016's safeguarding matters are open, and building a second product before the first has been delivered once would repeat the exact ordering error D-0092 already made. This is the answer to the year-from-now version of Hunter's worry, and it should stay parked until there is delivery experience to build it on.

4. Recommendation

Lead with Option A, uncapped. Design Option B deliberately. Park Option C — but know it is the real long-term answer.

Concretely: sell the half-day Foundations Session with an explicit multi-cohort pathway as the default commercial conversation — not a single session with a hopeful follow-up. If an organisation wants six cohorts, or ten, sell them six or ten. More cohorts in one organisation means more revenue and a better evidence position for the environment and shared-norm work, not a worse one. Offer the Extended Pilot Partnership to organisations that want depth and will participate in measurement, positioned honestly as data and implementation support, never as a booster.

Corrected 2026-08-09 — an earlier version recommended capping this at two to three cohorts per buyer. Withdrawn; see Option A's limit 2 for why it contradicted this record's own finding.

Stated plainly, because the independent review was right to push on it: this does not fully answer Hunter's worry. Option A defers the pigeonhole rather than removing it — it runs out when the organisation runs out of people. The genuine long-term answer is Option C — a real second product with genuinely different content (K-07's Stage 3 layer), which is the only one of the three that gives an existing participant an honest reason to come back. It stays parked because no pilot has run and D-0016 is open, not because it is the weaker idea. Revisit it the moment there is real delivery experience to build on.

What this recommendation does pass: it requires no efficacy claim MFC cannot support, which is the test D-0093 set.

5. What is genuinely open, and one thing that constrains all of it

  • Every option above is gated behind D-0016's six safeguarding matters, unchanged by this record. Nothing here brings participant-facing delivery closer to approved; it describes what the commercial model should be once that gate clears.
  • The pricing model needs recalculating for a half-day — facilitator hours, and therefore the cost basis and the base coverage fee. Not done here.
  • Multi-cohort pricing is undecided — whether a six-session commitment gets a volume rate, and what it is.
  • No buyer has ever been asked whether they would buy a multi-cohort pathway. Option A is strategically sound and commercially ordinary, but it is untested with a real MFC buyer, and the vault's own commercial research marks the workplace purchasing pathway as unknown.
  • Option A's limit is real: it does nothing for small organisations, which may be a large share of MFC's realistic early market.

Original source: 30-decisions/D-0094-half-day-format-and-repeat-engagement-model.md

D 0098 Introduction And Essentials Are Two Products

D-0098 — Two short formats, two jobs

The question

MFC has a built and tested 60-minute delivery kit. The offer ladder proposes a 90-minute Essentials as the paid entry product. Hunter asked whether Essentials should simply be the 60-minute kit that already exists, and delegated the call.

Decided

Both exist, and they are different products with different jobs. They are not two lengths of one thing — and treating them as such is what caused the confusion.

Introduction — 60 min Essentials — 90 min
Job Reach. People meet MFC and one person tries one thing A paid product. Someone bought it and expects something delivered
Where Amended 2026-08-10 (D2): adult community and workplace audiences, keynotes, conference and chamber slots. Schools and youth are excluded until C-16 closes and a safeguarding lead is named On site, a single organisation's team
Measurement Light only — not the full instrument Full, including the protected in-session block
Given back Nothing Amended 2026-08-10 (D2): a one-page team note to the room, no participant data. The "findings note to the organisation" is withdrawn — the reporting floor forbids participant data below 20 and every Essentials band is below it. Pooled cross-cohort findings once 20+ participants exist
Price Amended 2026-08-10 (D2): free as outreach, capped at 20/yr; $600 as a booked appearance ($400 was 1.05× loaded cost) STALE, superseded by D-0103 (2026-08-16) — current figures are $1,250 (2–5) / $1,550 (6–10) / $1,800 (11–15). ~~Amended 2026-08-10 (D2): $700 (2–5) / $950 (6–10) / $1,200 (11–15), in person. The old $450/$900 sold below or barely at loaded cost~~
Status Built and tested. Sellable now Designed; needs the final build pass

Why — structural, not preference

The measurement does not fit in sixty minutes. The forms draft protects ten in-session minutes for Form 2. Put that into the 60-minute kit and you have fifty minutes of teaching in a kit built for sixty — content cut to make room for data collection, in a format already tight.

At ninety minutes the same block is a far smaller proportion and the built content survives intact.

But that only matters if the session is a paid product — which exposes the real error: a reach format and a sellable format were being conflated. Nobody paid for a keynote and nobody receives a report from one, so it should not carry an instrument designed to produce one.

The product argument, stated separately from the behaviour-change one

Hunter asked for the call on product grounds, not only outcomes.

  • An hour is what you give an audience. Ninety minutes is what someone buys. Selling the give-away format creates exactly the ambiguity a founder hits walking into a local business — is this a talk, or is this training?
  • The extra thirty minutes is where the product stops being a demonstration. It buys running all three steps on the participant's own chosen moment rather than generically, plus the five public skills. That is the difference between watching the procedure and owning a rep.
  • MFC has something sellable immediately. The Introduction is built and tested, so it can be offered while the 90-minute build finishes. At zero paying customers, that matters.

What this changes

  1. The offer ladder gains an explicit line between the free/reach hour and the paid ninety.
  2. The measurement burden stops being forced into a format that cannot hold it — the Introduction carries a light set only, consistent with the forms draft's own narrower bar for the short format.
  3. Session-plan build work applies to Essentials at 90 minutes. The Introduction is not rebuilt.

What this does NOT change

D-0094's half-day Foundations is unaffected — its ~3 hours of content plus a break is the existing 3-hour build repackaged, not a new design. D-0016 still gates all participant-facing delivery. K-07 is untouched.

Where this could be wrong, and how it gets tested

If a small business owner says yes to an hour and balks at ninety minutes, the reach format has to become the product and the measurement has to shrink to fit.

The test is free: in the first three buyer conversations, ask for ninety minutes and record whether the pushback is about the length or the price. If it is consistently the length, this decision reverses and the instrument is redesigned for sixty.

Disclosure

No independent agent challenge was run on this record, and it should get one if it ever becomes load-bearing for a committee decision rather than an internal product call.

Original source: 30-decisions/D-0098-introduction-and-essentials-are-two-products.md

D 0091 Workshop Staged Arc And Team Pulse Compression

D-0091 — Workshop staged-arc exception and Team Pulse compression

Why this exists

Hunter, 2026-08-09, on D-0090's escalated recommendation to reopen Team Pulse: "i just don't know how we bring in the team pulse as we aren't doing 3-4 touch points now - the 2 products was a 1hr workshop and 3hr workshop." Then, directly: "i should see you complete the project on the workshop now."

Two things were open when he said that. Both resolve together, because they're the same underlying fact: MFC's live products are two standalone sessions, not a multi-touchpoint relationship.

1. The staged-arc conflict — resolved, written into K-07 directly

Flagged earlier the same session: K-07's staged teaching arc (D-0063) holds back full five-skill naming, State Check's full nuance, and three of the Shift menu's four options until "Stage 2 — Practising, early ongoing/online contact." The built 3-hour and 1-hour workshops teach all of this in full inside what the arc calls Stage 1.

Resolved as an exception, not a reversal. The arc's own logic — match content depth to the contact a person actually gets — was applied correctly by asking what contact MFC's real products actually offer. Both are standalone; there is no Stage 2 touchpoint most attendees ever reach. For a standalone Foundations Session specifically, Stage 1 and Stage 2 now collapse into one delivery moment in K-07 — full detail, reasoning and the boundary this does not move (Stage 3 stays held back) is written directly into K-07's staged-arc section, not duplicated here.

No change was needed to the workshop itself for this part. The workshop already teaches at Stage 1+2 depth; the framework record was the thing out of step, and it's now corrected.

2. Team Pulse — compressed into the two touchpoints that actually exist

D-0090 found the evidence-preferred mechanism for shifting norms in a group already exists in MFC's own source material (Team Pulse → Team Radar Snapshot → facilitated discussion → shared direction → observable practice → fortnightly review) and was shelved because it was designed for Offer 2's 3–4 touchpoint Implementation Pathway. That pathway is not what MFC runs. MFC runs one pre-session form, one session, and one post-session sequence (Form 2, Form 3, and — for case studies — the extended check-in D-0056 already approved). Team Pulse needed to be redesigned onto that shape, not deferred until a different product exists.

The redesign, mapped onto what already exists

Team Pulse step Where it now lives What changes
Private individual preference Form 1 (already collected before any teaching) One new nomination item, proposed not yet live — see workshop-package.html, "Our recommendation," item 08
Anonymous aggregate reveal In-session, at the existing Our-moments beat Facilitator aggregates Form 1 nominations beforehand and reveals the common themes live, anonymously — replacing the current mechanism, where each person privately guesses alone with no aggregation at all
Facilitated discussion → shared direction Same beat, extended by a few minutes The room is asked whether there's genuine appetite to agree on one shared practice — not assumed, asked
One observable practice, phrased as a commitment Same beat Phrased "we-if-then" (D-0090's adopted collective-implementation-intentions proposal), not a vague shared aspiration
Fortnightly review Already built — D-0056's case-study extended check-in and its fortnightly reminder/org check-in cadence No new mechanism needed; the existing case-study-only wave now has something specific to review

Explicitly not adopted: a genuine-agreement gate or safety screen. D-0090 already rejected this — a room without real appetite is told plainly it's fine to leave it, not pushed to a fake consensus. That instruction is written into the redesigned beat itself, not assumed.

Why this needs a facilitator prep step, stated honestly

Aggregating Form 1 nominations before the room requires the facilitator to do this between forms closing and the session starting. This is a real, new operational cost, not a free upgrade — small for a single session, but not zero, and it should be named rather than hidden inside "no participant friction." Participant-facing friction is genuinely unchanged: one additional form question, no new in-room burden beyond a few minutes of discussion that replaces private silent writing.

The 1-hour format — deliberately does less, not less-well

The 1-hour has no room for a live facilitated discussion. It keeps its existing, already-correct decision to decline working Our moments live, recorded as a named D-0014 deviation. What changes: the same Form 1 nomination question is still collected (it costs nothing extra — same form, both formats), and the facilitator can hand the host organisation what people privately said they'd want to work on together, even where there wasn't time to work it live. A smaller contribution, honestly smaller, not disguised as the full mechanism.

2a. Added 2026-08-09 — what "Team Pulse" actually means now, stated precisely for Hunter

Hunter, same day, a genuinely fair concern: "with the team pulse — we haven't figured out what that will be and how it runs." Checked directly against K-07 rather than assumed. Two different things share the name, and conflating them is exactly what produced the uncertainty:

What's actually built and live, right now: the compressed, in-session mechanism this section designed — private nomination via Form 1, anonymous aggregate reveal at 3:04, the room agreeing (or not) on one shared "when X, we will Y" commitment. It's in workshop-package.html today. This is what "Team Pulse" means inside the current product.

What was never built, and remains explicitly deferred: the source mechanism this borrowed its name and spirit from — Team Pulse → Team Radar Snapshot → facilitated discussion → shared direction → observable practice → fortnightly review → follow-up evaluation (Working Group 3, K-07's own Radar section). K-07 states this directly: "deliberately not adopted here... remains a working concept awaiting its own review." That status is unchanged by this record. Hunter's instinct that "how it runs" isn't fully figured out is correct for this bigger version — it was never meant to be resolved by the in-session compression above, and shouldn't be assumed solved.

The one real gap worth closing now, distinct from the bigger deferred mechanism: once a room agrees a shared commitment, nothing currently checks on it before Form 3 arrives at day 21–28. For an individual, a Mental Rep can fade the same way — but the workshop actively addresses that with a cue card and named barriers (3:22). The shared commitment gets none of that. Proposed, not yet built: a single templated reminder to whoever the room names as owning the commitment, sent around the Form 3 reminder infrastructure's own midpoint (roughly day 10–14) — the same wording the shared moment was recorded in, nothing more. This is deliberately not a facilitator touchpoint or a second product — it costs no delivery time, doesn't reopen D-0094/D-0095's ordering rule against building a second product before a pilot, and is closer to an email template than a design decision. Genuinely untested, and should be labelled as an attempt, not a proven reinforcement mechanism — consistent with D-0095's finding that reminder-style nudges show real-world effects far smaller than their appeal suggests.

Drafted, not yet wired into delivery infrastructure — since this is genuinely an email template rather than a design decision, drafting it is in the system's own remit and shouldn't wait on Hunter:

Subject: Quick check-in on [the shared commitment]

Hi [name],

A couple of weeks ago your team agreed: "[the exact wording the room recorded]."

Just a short check-in — how's it going? No need to report back, this is just a nudge to keep it live while it's still fresh.

— MFC

Send trigger and owner: attached to the same Form 3 reminder infrastructure, at its own midpoint (day 10–14), addressed to whoever the room named as owning the commitment at the time it was agreed — captured as part of the same in-session beat, not a separate data-collection step. Not yet wired into the actual Form 3 send mechanism — that integration work, and confirming the room actually names an owner reliably enough to send this to, is the one piece still open, and is better tested in a pilot than guessed at now.

3. What was implemented, not just decided

  • K-07's staged-arc section — the exception above, written directly (§1).
  • workshop-package.html, 3-hour Walkthrough — the Our-moments beat (3:04–3:16) redesigned to the aggregate-reveal-and-agree mechanism; Rationale & Evidence updated to cite the actual mechanism now taught, replacing the earlier citations that described the old private-write version.
  • workshop-package.html, Outcomes & Measurement — "Our recommendation" gains item 08 (the Form 1 nomination question) and the case-study "Case study" tab is updated to name what the extended check-in now specifically reviews.
  • The 1-hour Walkthrough and its own D-0014 deviation record are not changed in mechanism — only the shared framing (why it declines, and what it still collects) is clarified.

4. What this does not do

  • Does not claim organisational or cultural change from the standard pathway. The redesigned beat is still individual-self-report at every measured point except the shared practice's continuation, which only the case-study cohort's extended check-in reviews.
  • Does not add a fourth participant form. Same architecture as D-0056/D-0090 already settled: three forms for everyone, one case-study-only extended wave.
  • Does not resolve the genuine circularity D-0090 already named — psychological safety is both a precondition for honest group agreement and something the mechanism hopes to help build. Naming that a room can decline is the mitigation adopted, not a claim the circularity is closed.

5. Confidence and what remains unverified

High that this is the right compression of an evidence-preferred mechanism onto MFC's real product shape — it reuses infrastructure that already exists rather than inventing new touchpoints. Untested: no pilot has run this exact beat in either form, old or new. The facilitator-aggregation step has not been rehearsed. Whether a room genuinely reaches appetite for a shared practice, or mostly declines, is unknown either way.

Original source: 30-decisions/D-0091-workshop-staged-arc-and-team-pulse-compression.md

D 0110 Foundations Individual Teaching Not Environment Readiness

D-0110 — Foundations is individual teaching, not environment-readiness delivery, for now

The question this resolves

A 2026-08-27 bounded design panel (three per-product reviews plus a Compass founder-lens check) found that Foundations, as built, implicitly positions itself as the product that does the "environment and implementation conditions" job in MFC's three-part intervention model (KN-0006 part 3) — it is the only format with a team mechanism and the only one with room to spare — but does not actually deliver on that positioning. Compass's framing: "does Hunter want Foundations to go deeper on individual content, or actually become the format that does the organisational/leader readiness job — because right now it markets itself as the latter and delivers the former."

Hunter's instruction, 2026-08-27: "Take the Foundations question first."

Decision

For the current build cycle, Foundations' committed differentiator is the deepest individual teaching of the three formats — not organisational or environment-readiness delivery.

  1. The team-shared-commitment mechanism (D-0091's in-session Team Pulse compression, called Route B in the live facilitator guide) remains exactly as designed: a real, built capability, correctly gated in the current script behind a per-session requirement — "[GATE] Use only when the exact nomination item was approved, privacy-reviewed, collected and safely aggregated before the session" (20-half-day-foundations-facilitator-guide-current.md, 3:04–3:10 beat). Stated precisely, not overstated: that gate hasn't been cleared for the plain reason that MFC has never delivered any Foundations cohort at all yet — Route B hasn't specifically failed a review or been blocked, it simply hasn't been reached, and no standing process exists to clear it routinely once real delivery starts. This record does not remove, redesign, or devalue Route B. It stays built, available, and correctly gated.
  2. Route B is not to be treated, marketed, priced, or positioned as an active differentiator of the current Foundations product. Every real session, absent a specific, separately-approved privacy-reviewed nomination process for that specific engagement, runs Route A — private individual Radar, identical in kind to Essentials. That is the honest routine floor, and product positioning should say so.
  3. The team-nomination question on Form 1 (D-0091's "smaller, honestly smaller" contribution) stays exactly as designed: private signal-gathering that MFC can hand back to a host organisation, not an intervention and not claimed as one.
  4. This is a resourcing and sequencing decision, not a judgement that Route B is a bad idea. Building Route B into standing, routinely-cleared infrastructure — a repeatable privacy-review process, tested aggregation, a real cohort to run it on — is real, separate, uncosted work that a one-person charity with no cohort ever delivered should not take on inside this build cycle alongside everything else still open (safeguarding, clinical, privacy/legal, participant testing). Nothing here forecloses building it later, once a cohort has actually run and there is a reason to invest in the collective mechanism specifically.

Addendum, 2026-08-27 (same day) — extended to two more mechanisms found the same day

A reconciliation pass looking for other built-but-orphaned MFC design work (day-21 return session, Essentials leader briefing, manager-forum spec) found two more mechanisms in the identical category this record already covers — real, well-reasoned design work that gets ahead of what MFC can currently deliver, each written before this record existed and each never reconciled against it or against D-0105. Extending this record's logic explicitly rather than treating each as a fresh question:

  • The day-21 return session's IMPLEMENT branch (12-evidence-first-rebuild/120-RETURN-SESSION-DESIGN.md §6) — a collective team-Radar build that runs automatically once day-18 capture data crosses a threshold, with no per-engagement privacy-review gate analogous to Route B's. This is the same category of mechanism as Route B and is covered by this record on identical terms: real, stays designed, not integrated into the live candidate or run for a real cohort until it has the same gate Route B has (or a decision that supersedes this one). The return session's TEACH/PRACTICE branches are unaffected — individual teaching and practice content, exactly what this record says Foundations should be doing, and are cleared to integrate.
  • The manager forum and 12-month engagement specification (13-sustaining-practice-layer-v1/00-... and 01-...) — treats organisation/team-level, routinely running engagement as the normal shape of the product, and separately assumes a quarterly cadence for every engaged client that D-0105 (2026-08-21) restricts to selected case-study organisations only. Both conflicts predate this record and D-0105 respectively, and neither has been reconciled since. This specification stays explicitly out of scope for the live candidate — real, retained, not built into workshop-package.html as a standing offer. If pursued later, it needs to be re-scoped against both D-0105's case-study-only cadence and this record's individual-teaching commitment before it's positioned as anything a general client receives.

Nothing here forecloses either mechanism being built later, on the same terms as Route B — once a cohort has run and there's a specific, resourced reason to invest in the collective/organisational layer.

What this clarifies, and does not amend

D-0091 is unchanged. It correctly built the compressed Team Pulse mechanism and correctly recorded it as a real capability. This record does not reopen or weaken that work.

D-0092 is clarified, not amended. D-0092 justified Foundations' extension to a half-day partly "so the redesigned environment mechanism (D-0091's anonymous-reveal-and-agree beat) has real time to run properly." Read literally today, that framing implies the mechanism is a routine part of what a buyer gets — which is not accurate given the gate in point 1 above. D-0092's pricing and length decision itself is not reopened here (the extra time is used well regardless, per the 2026-08-27 panel's own finding that the half-day's genuine strengths — the engineered peak, the repeated teach-then-apply structure — are real and should not change). What's corrected is the reason given for part of that extra time: it should not be read as "this format routinely delivers collective/environment change," because it does not, absent a specific approved gate per engagement.

What a stronger version of "environment readiness" would need, if pursued later

Named here so it isn't lost, not because it's authorised now: a standing, repeatable privacy-review process for the Form 1 nomination-and-aggregation step (rather than a one-off per-engagement approval); a tested aggregation method; at least one real cohort where Route B actually ran, to know whether the mechanism works as designed; and a genuine leader/manager-facing component — none of which currently exists. This is future-facing context, not a commitment or a timeline.

Claim boundary

This record does not authorise describing Foundations, in any customer-facing material, as building team culture, organisational change, or environment readiness as a routine feature of the product. It authorises describing Foundations accurately: the deepest individual teaching of the three formats, with a genuine (but gated, not routine) option for a facilitated team moment where a specific engagement has separately cleared the privacy-review requirement. K-08 continues to govern all such statements.

Status

Decided. Implementation (workshop-package.html's decide3/outcomes3 tabs restated to reflect this positioning explicitly) follows in the same session this record was created.

Original source: 30-decisions/D-0110-foundations-individual-teaching-not-environment-readiness.md

D 0111 Product Architecture And Manager Session Unified

D-0111 — Product architecture and the unified manager session

Decision

1. ~~The three products are not one architecture at three lengths — Introduction is genuinely different in kind~~

[!warning] SUPERSEDED 2026-08-31 by Hunter's direct instruction. §1 no longer holds.

Hunter, 2026-08-31: "So I think for all products - we have a similar flow or narrative that we follow - the longer the session the more depth and info we can share (& practice)." Shown this clause afterwards, he was explicit: "introduction is not a different design brief. Change that."

What now holds: all three products follow one shared narrative — the same beats, in the same order. Duration buys depth, information and practice volume, not a different structure. Introduction is the shortest expression of the same journey, not a separate design brief. Recorded in 60-projects/workshop-evidence-informed-adult/15-current-service-definition-v1/37-WORKSHOP-NARRATIVE-SPINE-v2.md.

What survives unchanged: that Essentials and Foundations are a depth ladder on a shared thesis — correct then, correct now, and now extended to cover Introduction as well. §2 onward of this decision is unaffected.

Consequence not to be missed: §1's resolution of finding 6 of the 2026-08-27 contrarian review no longer stands. That finding is reopened, and the contrarian's "one loop taught three times at increasing dosage" characterisation is now closer to the intended design than this record's rejection of it was.

Superseded text preserved below, per this vault's convention of superseding rather than deleting.

Introduction (60 min) is a standalone, portable talk — deliverable to any organisation, any team, any ages, with no institutional infrastructure behind it (no return session, no data capture, no environment work). Its design centre of gravity is narrative and explanation, not experience: theory, story, and connection, structured to answer one question directly — in one hour, with no follow-up of any kind, what gives someone the greatest realistic chance of starting a genuinely independent, lifelong practice on their own. This is a different design brief from Essentials and Foundations, not a shorter version of the same one.

Essentials (90 min) and Foundations (half-day) share one core thesis, theory, and method. They are not different jobs — they are the same job at different depth and time. Foundations is Essentials plus the additional element the half-day's extra time genuinely allows (per D-0110, that extra element is deeper individual teaching, not routine organisational delivery). Within that shared architecture: go deeper on some things in Foundations than Essentials allows time for (Hunter's own example: more depth on Stop-Shift-Do specifically in Foundations than Essentials), but the main thesis and how it's taught stays the same across both — this is a depth ladder between these two specifically, not a redesign at each length.

What Essentials/Foundations are actually for, stated in Hunter's own terms: less time for the slow, experiential pacing Foundations can afford — not fewer reps, not less practice, just less time spent taking people through it slowly — traded for more explanation of why it matters and where it counts, so the room can properly set up a real plan together. The point for the room as a whole is a genuine "we all want this together" moment and a plan built collectively for that team/organisation, not just individual practice sitting inside a shared room.

This directly resolves finding 6 of the 2026-08-27 contrarian review (three-product-content pass): the products are not simply "one loop taught three times at increasing dosage." Introduction is a genuinely different design brief. Essentials and Foundations are a depth ladder on a shared thesis — that part of the contrarian's "dosage ladder" characterisation was correct for those two, and is now confirmed as the intended design, not an unexamined default.

2. The manager/leader session is unified: one real ~1-hour session, shared across Essentials and Foundations

This corrects work done earlier the same day. The 45-minute, Essentials-only leader briefing integrated into workshop-package.html (id="leader90") this morning does not match this decision and is superseded, pending a rebuild — see "What this supersedes" below.

The manager/leader session must be:

  1. ~1 hour, not 45 minutes. Hunter's own words: "it needs its own product... we need them to fully be across it, to fully understand it, to be bored in [drawn in]... we can't just go tick in the box half an hour." A shorter session reads, and functions, as a compliance formality rather than genuine engagement — Hunter is explicit that this is the wrong shape regardless of how well the content inside it is designed.
  2. One shared session for both Essentials and Foundations buyers, not a separate design per product. The manager's job is materially the same regardless of which team session their people attend.
  3. Content emphasis, stated directly: - What to actually watch for in the people they manage — signals, not just categories. - How this gets implemented concretely in their existing team rhythms: team meetings, whether a recurring slot (Hunter's example: a Friday session) can carry it, physical/environmental reminders (posters or equivalent), each built with real intention rather than bolted on. - Framed as the manager's own responsibility to upskill on — not only "this helps you and your own life," but explicitly "this is a responsibility you and your team carry, and here's what to be mindful of and how to build that skill."
  4. A proper meeting, a proper conversation — the register Hunter wants is genuine engagement and dialogue, not a scripted briefing delivered at a manager.

3. A separate, later idea — not authorised or built now

Hunter named a further concept, explicitly distinct from the ~1-hour session above and not something to build in this pass: a lighter, recurring (fortnightly) ~30-minute manager/CEO community session — quick, simple, educational updates on MFC's recommendations for managers and CEOs, why the problem is hard, and what they can do about it. Hunter connected this directly to conversations already had with Eimear Quigley, Debra Fiddler, Nabil, and Alysse Curran (Head of Brand). This is the same territory the already-discovered, deliberately-not-integrated manager forum spec (13-sustaining-practice-layer-v1/00-.../01-...) occupies, at a different (fortnightly, not quarterly) cadence than that spec currently proposes. Not authorised for build in this record — named here so it isn't lost, consistent with D-0110's treatment of the same spec as real, retained, future-facing work.

4. What remains genuinely open — Hunter's own thought, not completed

Hunter was mid-sentence, actively working out the day-21 return session's exact content mechanism, when the message ended: whether the return should (a) capture data right before the session and build the conversation from what's captured, (b) go into more depth re-explaining the material as a reinforced reminder, (c) function specifically as a check-in, or some combination — his own words trail off at "or is it specifically around...". This record does not answer that question or guess at where Hunter's sentence was going. It stays open, and should be asked back to him directly rather than inferred, per CLAUDE.md §6a condition 1 (essential information does not yet exist — here because the person supplying it hadn't finished supplying it).

What this supersedes, and what it doesn't

Supersedes, pending rebuild: the leader90 tab in workshop-package.html (45-minute, Essentials-only leader briefing, integrated 2026-08-27 morning) no longer matches product architecture. It is not deleted — it remains visible, marked superseded, until the ~1-hour shared version replaces it.

Does not supersede or reopen: D-0110 (Foundations is individual-teaching-focused, Route B stays gated) — this record is consistent with and clarifies D-0110, it does not reopen the question D-0110 settled. The day-21 TEACH/PRACTICE content already integrated stays as-is; only the manager-session shape and the open day-21-mechanism question are affected here. The contrarian review's other findings (the Stop-Shift-Do two-step question, the Radar narrowing-risk disclosure gap, the cue-mechanism rehearsal gap) are unaffected by this record and remain open for separate resolution.

Claim boundary

Unchanged from prior records in this series: this record authorises product architecture and design intent. It does not authorise any claim of effectiveness, organisational change, or manager behaviour change from a session that has never been run. K-08 continues to govern any external-facing statement.

Status

Decided on products 1–3 above. Implementation (rebuilding the manager session as a shared ~1-hour tab, marking leader90 superseded) is the next concrete step. Item 4 remains open pending Hunter completing his own stated thought.

D 0112 Single Takehome Leavebehind And Route B Reframe

D-0112 — One take-home leave-behind, not separate cards; Route B simplified to agreement, not live design

The problem Hunter named directly

The current build issues up to eight separate per-person printed items (disclosure card, skills card, SSD card, HOS sheet, State Check card, shift-toolkit sheet, Radar worksheet, cue card). Hunter's own words: "I don't know if we have a cue card... that just means they need to be bringing paper, which is an extra cost for us, and they're probably just gonna chuck it in the bin... that's the truth." The realistic failure mode is cost without retention — printed pieces people don't carry and don't keep.

Separately, Hunter does not want Route B (the shared/collective room-agreement moment) disabled, but reframed: not the room co-designing new commitments live, but a simple, repeated "do we agree we want this, understand it, value it" — and, where a cohort has that context, selecting from implementation options already worked out with managers beforehand, not inventing new ones live.

Decision

1. One consolidated take-home leave-behind replaces the separate reference cards

The disclosure card, skills card, SSD card, HOS sheet, State Check card and cue card are replaced by one single folded leave-behind per person — a real "cheat sheet," not several loose items: one panel per short reference (skills, SSD, State Check), and a scan/QR link encouraging participants to complete their Radar on the MFC website. One object, sized to survive a desk drawer, not a stack of cards.

Corrected 2026-08-27, same day, direct from Hunter: the leave-behind is premade and identical for every participant — nothing is written on it. The if/then cue ("when X, I will Y") is written on the participant's own phone (a note, reminder, or saved message), not on any physical object. The fold-and-hold physical ritual folds the premade leave-behind exactly as printed; the gesture, not an act of personal writing, is what closes that beat. The first draft of this record wrongly described a write-in space on the leave-behind — this section supersedes that description.

Not affected: the Radar worksheet (A4, substantive, already theirs to keep) and the two measure forms (data collection, not reference material) stay separate as before. The shift-toolkit sheet's content, where still delivered, folds into the same single leave-behind rather than staying a separate sheet.

Butcher's paper stays exactly as already designed for in-session writing (individual or shared, per the existing Route A/B split) — this record does not touch that mechanism, only the take-home object.

2. Route B reframed: agreement and predetermined-choice, not live co-design

Route B is not disabled by this record — it remains gated exactly as D-0110/D-0111 already established (no shared/aggregate moment runs until the team-nomination module is separately privacy-reviewed and approved per engagement). What changes, for when it is cleared to run: the room is not asked to invent a new shared commitment live. It is asked two simpler things, repeated at the start, middle and end of the session in Hunter's own words — "do we all agree that we all want this, that we understand it, that we can value it" — and, where the cohort's managers have already selected implementation options beforehand (e.g. "every Friday" or "end of each team meeting"), the room chooses which of those predetermined options they're most likely to actually follow through on. This is evidence-aligned specificity ("this is what we do, and we're incorporating this") rather than a vague suggestion ("go for a walk").

Framing discipline, repeated throughout the session per Hunter's direction: the session states plainly, more than once, what this is and isn't — mental fitness, not "all about mental health" or "emotional openness." That distinction is not new content; it restates the existing claims-boundary discipline (K-08) as an explicit, repeated in-room line rather than an implicit design choice.

What this does not change

  • Does not reopen D-0110 (Foundations remains individual-teaching-focused; Route B stays gated on the same terms).
  • Does not reopen D-0111 (product architecture, manager-session unification unaffected).
  • Does not authorise Route B to run for any cohort without its existing privacy-review gate cleared.

Claim boundary

Authorises materials and room-design changes only. Does not authorise any claim that the consolidated leave-behind or the reframed agreement moment improves retention, follow-through, or organisational outcomes — untested, as with every other mechanism in this build. K-08 continues to govern all external-facing statements.

Status

Decided. Implementation (workshop-package.html materials lists, cue-selection beats, and the Route B beat description) follows in the same session this record was created.

Original source: 30-decisions/D-0112-single-takehome-leavebehind-and-route-b-reframe.md

D 0113 Product Boundary Everything Inside The Price

D-0113. What the price buys

The decision

The three-week return session, the written report to the organisation, and the manager session all sit INSIDE the product price. They are not optional extensions, not separately contracted, and not separately quoted.

The manager session is not separately priced. D-0111 records Hunter saying it "needs its own product"; that is confirmed as a statement about the session's design seriousness and shared shape across both products, not about its commercial packaging. It remains bundled.

Prices are unchanged and were never in question: Foundations $3,900 base + $95 per person, cap 20; Essentials $1,250 (2-5) / $1,550 (6-10) / $1,800 (11-15); Introduction $600 booked or free as capped outreach. Founder decision 2026-08-16, recorded in D-0103 and the Product and Pricing Book.

Why this was needed

On 29 August three service packs were written (maintained_by: Codex, status proposed_for_hunter_decision) defining each product's teachable core, with "core exclusions" that placed the manager component, the return contact and the routine data/report outside it. Independent verification on 2026-08-30 found:

  • Read as a commercial boundary, those exclusions would move 8.25 to 9.25 of Foundations' 15.75 costed facilitator hours (52% to 59%) and 3.5 to 3.75 of Essentials' 8.25 hours (42% to 46%) outside the priced product.
  • The exclusions do not originate in D-0110 or D-0111. D-0110 excludes only the return session's IMPLEMENT branch and states the TEACH/PRACTICE branches "are cleared to integrate"; D-0111 upgrades rather than removes the manager session.
  • The commercial reading was nonetheless stated, not merely implied, in 24-MEASURED-SERVICE-EXTENSIONS-v3.md ("sellable candidate versions… alongside—not inside—the learning minutes"; manager components recorded as not purchased / offered / delivered).
  • No occurrence anywhere in the vault prices the manager session separately. FINAL-02-pricing-strategy.md line 65 carries a Leaders' Session row, but its price column reads "Included" and its $139 is a cost figure. Everywhere else it is costed only as an input, at 1.5 facilitator hours inside both products.

So a component had been described as separately purchasable without ever becoming a line item, while remaining charged for invisibly inside two products.

Rationale

The return and the report are the product, not extras. The Product and Pricing Book's competitive defence rests on them: 5.25 participant-contact hours at $92.38 per person per contact hour at a ten-person cohort ($67.62 at fifteen), compared against a $3,500-$7,500 in-house Mental Health First Aid class. Stripping the return and report reduces that to 4.0 contact hours and the differentiation argument goes with it.

Reopening the price was explicitly rejected. It is decided, single-valued, correct in the paper the committee holds, and sits before them as ask 1 of 4. No buyer has ever been quoted anything. Reopening a correct price to resolve an internal documentation inconsistency would spend founder and committee credibility on a problem no external party has seen.

Consequences and required propagation

  1. The 29 August service packs remain valid as facilitator scoping (what happens in the room) and are declined as a commercial boundary. Their "core exclusions" wording must be qualified so it cannot be read as a pricing or contracting statement.
  2. 24-MEASURED-SERVICE-EXTENSIONS-v3.md's not purchased manager-component status is superseded; the manager session is always included.
  3. Stale worked examples computed from the superseded $3,500 base were corrected in 110-product-pricing-onepager.html on 2026-08-30 ($4,450 → $4,850, $4,925 → $5,325, $328 → $355 per person).
  4. FINAL-06-two-product-model.md still carries the superseded pair in ten places, and FINAL-09-committee-review.md records a downstream arithmetic error ($5,000 − $4,450 stated as $930; the true difference at the current $4,850 is $150). Open.
  5. FINAL-02-pricing-strategy.md remains stale on $2,500/$1,367. Open.
  6. The Hub pricing and workshop-delivery projections need regenerating. The Hub integrity check was failing on unrelated structural drift as at 2026-08-30.

What this decision does not do

It does not ratify any price. Committee approval of ask 1 remains outstanding and is a real external gate. It is not market validation: no buyer has paid any price and zero cohorts have run. It does not clear delivery, which remains blocked on the escalation and distress-response procedures.

Unit economics, confirmed 2026-08-30

The manager session was already inside the price. It is costed as 1.5 facilitator hours in Foundations (of 15.75) and 1.5 in Essentials (of 8.25). D-0111's upgrade from 45 to 60 minutes adds 0.25 hours, $16.53 per run at $66.10, or $23.14 loaded. No price increase is warranted.

Precision note on that +0.25. It is verified for Essentials: D-0111 supersedes a 45-minute Essentials-only briefing with a ~1 hour session, and the Book's 1.5 hours implies roughly 0.75 delivery plus 0.75 prep, so a 15-minute delivery extension adds exactly 0.25. It is assumed for Foundations, where no source states the leader session was ever 45 minutes. The assumption errs conservative (it overstates cost). It may also understate, because D-0111 asks for "a proper meeting, a proper conversation" with manager-specific implementation planning, which is plausibly more prep rather than only more delivery. Unifying one design across both products is a build-time saving, not a per-run one, so no per-run credit is taken. The swing either way is roughly $16 to $50 a run against $3,000+ retained cash, so the conclusion holds under every reading.

D 0114 Return Session Is A Checkin Branching Design Retired

D-0114. The return session is a check-in

The decision

The return session exists because a skill decays if nobody comes back. It is a check-in, not a second lesson and not a drill.

The first twenty minutes are identical for Essentials and Foundations: what today is, the room's own picture from session one (aggregate, no names, no counts), warm reps with an opt-out, then whatever participants said they most wanted to learn or were finding hard. Then Essentials goes deeper into understanding and practice, and Foundations goes into how the team implements it together.

Retired, in full: the TEACH / PRACTICE / IMPLEMENT classification; the six modules; the five allocation rules and percentage thresholds; the eight-response floor; the fewer-than-five rule; candidate shared moments composed offline at day 19 to 20; and the private paper slip vote with its veto box and disposal protocol.

Why

Hunter, 2026-08-30, verbatim: "I don't agree with the eight response floor... It should just be got four people. This is what we're doing with you. We're here to help. This isn't about, like, we gotta keep a fuck because this is crazy or really scary. We're not trying to capture. Is it a bad workplace? Tell us, be honest. It's like, hey, what are the things that you wanna work on as a group... If we can keep things digital, we can keep things simple."

The reasoning, stated so it is not lost: the anonymity apparatus was built for a disclosure question, and the question actually being asked is a positive one. A secret ballot around "what shall we practise together" signals danger the question does not carry, and so creates the fear it was meant to manage. The scope rule is retained: anything really about workload, safety, staffing or how one person behaves is not a shared moment and goes to the enabling-conditions column as a category. This record originally claimed the scope rule alone did the protective work the ballot had been carrying. The 2026-08-30 safeguarding review found that wrong — see the addendum. A private route to remove a candidate is retained, as a spoken costless exit rather than paper.

Second reason, delivery. The retired design asked one facilitator who has never rehearsed the session to classify a cohort, choose among six modules against five rules, compose candidates offline, run a paper ballot and sequence a leader beat, inside seventy-five minutes. That is a protocol, not a service. Every conditional branch is something that can fail live in front of a first paying customer.

Retained from the retired design

The reason the return exists; the leader beat and its single question ("which one of these can you make true, and by when?", asking for a commitment and a date, not a verdict); the scope rule on what cannot be a shared moment; aggregate-only reporting; and the rule that nothing an individual wrote is visible when a leader enters.

Two safeguards attached at the same time

  1. The pre-session form goes to MFC, never to the manager. An employee telling their employer through MFC that they are struggling is a disclosure inside an employment relationship. The manager receives themes.
  2. Data shown back to the room carries no counts, at any group size. "Handovers came up, and a couple of people caught it at the time" is fine. "Two of you tried it" is not, because in a small room the arithmetic identifies people whatever words surround it. Corrected 2026-08-30 after the safeguarding review — this originally read as a wording test, which cannot catch an arithmetic failure. See the addendum.

Price and length consequence, modelled and deliberately not applied

Extending the Essentials return from thirty to sixty minutes adds about 0.75 of a facilitator hour. The Pricing Book costs Essentials at 8.25 hours; D-0113 adds 0.25 for the longer manager session, giving 8.5; this change adds 0.75, giving 9.25 hours, direct cost $671.43 and loaded $940.00 against the book's $605 and $847. Retained margin at the middle band falls from 61% to 57%; roughly $100 across the bands ($1,350 / $1,650 / $1,900) would restore it.

Not applied. The committee is asked on 31 August 2026 to adopt the current prices. This returns to them as a product improvement once built. D-0113 continues to govern what the price includes, and nothing here changes it.

Essentials moves from 2.0 to 2.5 hours of participant contact, closing the gap to Foundations from 2.6x to 2.1x, so Foundations earns its price on the depth of its teaching, the on-site return and the written report rather than on time. D-0110 forbids positioning the team-shared mechanism as an active differentiator while its approval gate is open, so the collective piece is not the commercial argument.

What this decision does not do

It does not clear delivery. The escalation and distress-response procedures still do not exist in cleared form, so no facilitator, including Hunter, can be cleared to deliver. It is not evidence: no return session of any design has ever been run or rehearsed, and whether one contact inside the decay window is enough remains unevidenced.

Addendum, 2026-08-30: what the safeguarding review changed

The retirement of the classification, the six modules, the percentage rules, the paper ballot ceremony and the response floor on the team beat all stand. Three things in this record's own reasoning did not survive an adversarial read and are corrected in 121:

  1. "A sentence test replaces the response floor" was wrong. A wording test cannot catch an arithmetic failure. At three people, "two of you tried it" identifies the third by subtraction however carefully it is phrased. The fix is not a floor: it is no counts at any group size. Show what happened, never how many. That protects every room identically and never tells a small team it is too small for something.
  2. "The scope rule does the ballot's work" was wrong. They protect different people from different things. The scope rule governs what may be proposed; the ballot let one person remove a candidate without arguing for it in front of colleagues. Without a private route, dissent in a team of four is fully attributable and the predictable outcome is silence, a surviving candidate and a scheduled commitment several people privately object to. Reinstated as a spoken, costless exit ("tell me at the break, I'll take it off and I won't say who"), which is lighter than the paper it replaces.
  3. The form routing rule was right but incomplete. It needed a participant- facing boundary line, the restored promise that the organisation gets nothing about what anyone answered, a stated reader and deletion rule, and an honest statement that the form is not monitored. It also collides with 110's rule that the capture never reaches the organisation; that conflict is now stated rather than silently reconciled.

Also caught, and not covered by any of the three claims: simplification had made answering aloud the default with no opt-out, which breaches K-08 rule 6. The leader-free requirement for the team beat had been dropped. The D-0110 approval gate was cited in metadata and contradicted in the body. And the enabling-conditions column, which leaders see, had no de-identification standard beyond "no names". All are fixed in 121.

121 Return Session Design V2

The return session, v2

1. Why we come back at all

A skill that is learned once and never revisited is expected to decay. That is the reason this session exists. How much it decays, and whether one contact inside the window is enough, is not established (see section 6). It is not a second lesson, and it is not a drill.

It is a check-in. People come back, see what they and the room actually did, get an answer to the thing they most wanted to know, and leave with the practice alive rather than filed.

Founder framing, 2026-08-30, verbatim: "we're not trying to capture. Is it a bad workplace? Tell us, be honest. It's like, hey, what are the things that you wanna work on as a group... we wanna help people. This isn't just about making the most profitable product."

2. The shape: same opening for both products

The first twenty minutes of the Essentials and Foundations returns are identical. One design, delivered twice.

Who is in the room for it. Participants only. No manager, leader or host is present for the opening twenty minutes of either return, including the Essentials return, which is online. The host is admitted at the point the design says so and not before. If a leader will not leave or cannot be excluded from the call, the room's own picture is not shown and the session moves straight to practice. Do not explain why in front of them.

0 to 3 minutes: what today is

Say what this is: a check-in on what they have actually done since, not a test and not a new lesson.

3 to 8 minutes: here is what you did

Show the room what happened since session one. Plainly and positively: the kinds of moment that came up, that some people caught them at the time, that some people tried something.

The rule, and it replaces the retired response floor. Show what happened. Never how many.

  • "Handovers came up, and a couple of people caught it at the time" — yes.
  • "Two of you tried it" — no. No counts, no fractions, no percentages, no "most of you", at any group size.

Why this is a ban on numbers rather than a minimum group size. A count is arithmetic, and in a small room arithmetic identifies people whatever words surround it. In a group of three, "two of you tried it" names the third by subtraction, and no phrasing prevents it. Removing the denominator removes the exposure, and it does so identically at every group size, so no room is ever told it is too small for something.

Also never: attribute a moment, quote anyone, or single out one unattributed act for praise in a small room, because the room will assign it to a person and mark by contrast whoever it decides did not do it.

8 to 14 minutes: warm reps

Three short scenarios, answered as Stop, Shift, Do.

Nobody is required to speak. Offer, out loud and before starting, that people may answer aloud, answer quietly with the person next to them, or think it through alone — then take answers only from whoever offers. Below six people, default to quiet pairs or private thinking. K-08 rule 6 forbids forcing public sharing and rule 4 requires a built-in opt-out; this beat is not an exception to either.

14 to 20 minutes: the thing you asked about

At the end of session one, or by a short form about a week before this session, everyone is asked one question: what is one more thing you would like to learn, or one thing you are finding hard?

Whatever comes up most, we cover here. Not an algorithm, not a classification. They tell us, and we bring it.

What the form must carry, in the participant's sight, before they answer:

This comes to us, not to your workplace. Your organisation gets nothing about what any of you answered — no quotes, no individuals, no breakdown by team, shift, site or role. Only an MFC facilitator reads it, and it is deleted once this session has run. It is not a support channel and it is not monitored day to day. If something needs help now, [referral line].

Unresolved conflict, stated rather than reconciled (CLAUDE.md §4). 110 states as a standing rule that the between-session capture never reaches the commissioning organisation at any group size. It is not settled whether this form is that same instrument or a second one, nor whether anything derived from it may go to the organisation at all. Until that is resolved, nothing from this form goes to the organisation, and themes from it are not part of the written report.

Why "themes to the manager" is not by itself a privacy control. In a team of four, a theme is often the same content with the pronoun removed, and the manager can usually work out who. 110's themes-not-participant-data rule exists to stop small groups being treated worse; it is not a finding that themes are safe at small numbers.

3. Then the two products diverge

Essentials, the remaining 40 minutes

More understanding, and more practice. Go deeper on whatever they asked for, then run reps on it. Two or three rounds, in pairs, on supplied scenarios, with quiet or solo options offered aloud so that taking one is invisible.

Essentials ends there, with people having practised the thing they said they wanted to work on. No claim is made that they are now better at it.

Foundations, the remaining 55 minutes

Everything above, plus the collective piece: how this team does it together.

[GATE] This beat does not run unless three things are true. The leaders are out of the room and stay out. D-0110's per-engagement approval for the team-nomination item has been obtained for this engagement. And the candidate material was collected and safely aggregated beforehand. If any is not true, substitute practice, and do not say why in the room.

Choosing what the team works on, 20 minutes. Put four or five candidate moments in front of the room, drawn from what people have already said. Talk about it. Agree two, each with one observable move.

The costless exit, said out loud before the discussion starts:

"If any of these doesn't sit right with you, tell me at the break or on the way out. I'll take it off, and I won't say who or why."

Removal is unconditional and unattributed, including a candidate MFC wrote. This replaces the retired paper ballot and does the one thing the ballot was actually for: letting a person remove something without arguing for it in front of colleagues. It matters most in small teams, where spoken dissent is fully attributable and permanently remembered, and where the alternative is silence followed by a commitment several people privately object to. No shared moment is better than a false one.

The scope rule. If something is really about workload, safety, staffing, or how one person behaves, it is not a shared moment. Say so plainly in the room: "that one isn't ours to fix with a habit", and put it in the enabling-conditions column as a category.

How that column is written, because leaders see it. Categories in general terms, no names, and nothing so specific that one person's role, shift or site identifies them. "Handover time" is a category; "time to hand over properly on night shift" identifies whoever works nights.

[NEVER] describe or record the enabling-conditions column, the team Radar, or anything else in this session as a psychosocial hazard control, a hazard identification, or anything an employer may rely on to discharge a duty.

Placing them, 15 minutes. Each of the two moments gets a named routine that already happens, a named person who starts it, a ten-second description, and a review date agreed in the room. A team that agrees two moves and does not place them in something that already exists has produced a decision that evaporates.

The leaders, last 20 minutes. They join at the end, having not been in the room before it. They receive the enabling-conditions column, and each answers one question out loud, in one sentence:

"Which one of these can you make true, and by when?"

Ask for the commitment and the date, not a verdict. "Yes, we support that" is free.

Before they come in: anything an individual wrote is off the walls and off the tables. Categories only.

4. What this design deletes, and why

Removed Why
TEACH / PRACTICE / IMPLEMENT classification We ask people what they want instead of sorting them
Six modules and five allocation rules A solo facilitator who has never run this cannot carry a decision tree live
The eight-response floor on the team beat Built for a disclosure question. The question is "what shall we work on together"
Private paper slips, the veto box, the disposal protocol Ceremony that signalled danger the question does not carry. The veto itself is retained as a spoken, costless exit
Candidate moments composed offline at day 19 to 20 as a hard gate Candidates now come from what people have already told us, and the room talks about them

Deliberately NOT deleted, and reinstated here after the 2026-08-30 safeguarding review: small-number protection when showing the room its own data, now expressed as a ban on counts rather than a group-size floor; the private route to remove a candidate; the leader-free requirement for the team beat; and the opt-out on speaking aloud.

Kept from v1: the reason the return exists; the leader commitment with a date; the scope rule; aggregate-only reporting; and the rule that nothing individual is visible when a leader enters.

5. Length and price consequence

Extending the Essentials return from thirty to sixty minutes adds about 0.75 of a facilitator hour (half an hour of delivery, a quarter for preparing what they asked for).

The baseline, stated so the arithmetic can be followed. The Product and Pricing Book costs Essentials at 8.25 hours. D-0113 adds 0.25 for the manager session moving from forty-five to sixty minutes, giving 8.5. This change adds a further 0.75, giving 9.25 hours, direct cost $671.43 and loaded $940.00 against the book's 8.25-hour figures of $605 and $847.

At current prices the middle band's retained margin falls from 61% to 57%. Restoring it would take about $100 across the bands, to $1,350 / $1,650 / $1,900 (modelled 2026-08-30 from the Product and Pricing Book's own rate and multiplier).

Not applied. The committee is being asked on 31 August to adopt the current prices, and this change comes back to them as a product improvement once it is built. D-0113 governs what the price includes; nothing here changes it.

One effect worth seeing. Essentials goes from 2.0 to 2.5 hours of participant contact, so the gap to Foundations closes from 2.6x to 2.1x. Foundations then earns its price on the depth of its teaching, the on-site return and the written report. D-0110 forbids positioning the team-shared mechanism as an active differentiator while its approval gate is open, so the collective piece is not the commercial argument.

6. What is still unknown, and what blocks delivery

Nothing here has been run or rehearsed. No return session of any design ever has.

Specifically unevidenced, and it must be said that way: whether one contact inside the decay window is enough or two would be better; whether peer correction against a short rubric is any good; and whether a facilitated team agreement survives three weeks. These are reasoned judgements placed where the transfer literature points, not findings.

Blockers, in full rather than by implication:

  1. The escalation and distress-response procedures do not exist in cleared form. No facilitator, including Hunter, can be cleared to deliver until they do. This covers written disclosure arriving on the pre-session form as much as disclosure in the room.
  2. D-0016's six safeguarding matters remain unresolved, and D-0099 changed how that gate is framed without resolving any of them. Escalation wording is one of the six, not the whole set.
  3. D-0110's per-engagement approval gate on the team-nomination mechanism is open, so the collective piece is designed but not cleared to run.
  4. This document has had internal AI review only. The clinical governance, legal and privacy, and insurance gates are all open. Nothing in this file is clearance.

What actually changed, in one paragraph

Four product-architecture decisions landed (D-0109–D-0112): WHO-5 made routine, Foundations repositioned as individual teaching not organisational readiness, the three products' architecture clarified (Introduction is a standalone talk; Essentials/Foundations share one thesis at different depth), and the take-home leave-behind redesigned around how people actually behave (premade, cue written on their own phone, not a card nobody carries). A three-way debate on core-session time allocation was reconciled and independently checked (a real contradiction was caught and fixed before it reached Hunter). A four-pass build-readiness audit then found: session-script content is built for all three products; visual/print production and facilitator-training/safeguarding procedures are MISSING for all three, and the second is a hard blocker — no facilitator, including Hunter, can currently be cleared to deliver, because the required escalation/distress procedures don't exist. A first draft of those procedures was written (not cleared — needs qualified clinical/legal review). The manager session was rebuilt to the new shared ~1hr spec. Two slide decks were built from scratch (Introduction, Essentials — neither existed before). Content was added addressing participants who already meditate/journal, plus a comprehension check. Every substantive change went through an independent fresh-context check before landing; several real defects were caught and fixed this way (see "What broke and was fixed" below).

  6. Hunter's own sign-off, per product — the dashboard's gate, locked until an independent check and a real rehearsal both exist for that product.

Governance notes for whoever picks this up

This vault runs a mandatory routing-record system (.claude/hooks/enforce_material_specialist_closure.py) — any material change must be closed with a schema-v2 routing record via 90-meta/full-permanent-specialist-bench-v1/make_routing_record.py, and topic state changes go through 90-meta/controlled-automation-v1/topic-control/record_topic_reconciliation.py, which also regenerates the Hub. If you're working outside Claude Code's hook environment (e.g. a different tool or Codex directly), these hooks won't fire automatically — but the underlying discipline (real independent check before anything reaches Hunter, honest disclosure of what's untested, no claim beyond what evidence supports) is the actual standard this vault runs on, hooks or not.
