24 Half Day Specialist Panel And Architecture Decision

Half-Day Foundations — specialist-lens synthesis and architecture recommendation

Contract audit, 13 August 2026: this was one producing context applying seventeen professional role lenses, one restricted screen and one same-context reconciliation. It changed the real artifact and remains useful design evidence, but it did not preserve one task packet and contract-complete output per specialist. It is therefore not a completed bounded or independent multi-specialist panel.

Sequencing addendum, 20 August 2026: A-24 (Quinn) ran inside this same-context panel as one lens among nineteen (see "Learning, behaviour and participant experience" below), not as a pre-dispatch coverage challenge gating the other eighteen. The standard this panel is judged against later made that ordering binding as L-066 (design-intelligence-and-founder-finalisation-standard.md, written 2026-08-15, two days after this panel ran): "the coverage challenge is a precondition of the first Agent call, not a step in the plan... once reviews are in flight the challenge has nothing left to gate and silently degrades into a review of the output." That is exactly what happened here, and per L-066 rule 2 it is recorded as a genuine ordering violation, not retrofitted as compliant — completed_before_execution: false for this panel (see this record's routing record). The real, valid pre-dispatch-equivalent correction is a separate document produced the same day, assurance-2026-08-13/coverage-challenge.md — a genuinely independent, contract-complete A-24 output that named this exact defect ("the existing same-context synthesis... records zero bounded specialist reviews and zero independent specialist reviews") and drove the two staged panels (assurance-2026-08-13/, assurance-2026-08-13-evaluated-panel/) later reconciled in 25-half-day-whole-bench-reconciliation-and-closure.md. Read this document's architecture table below as informed by a coverage challenge that happened correctly in that sibling file, not inside this one.

Founder summary

The current Half-Day is not a bad workshop and it does not need to be rebuilt from zero. It has a strong human premise, a coherent three-block journey, meaningful practice, careful boundaries and substantial prior research. The weakness is more specific: it still behaves too often like a well-explained curriculum followed by activities, rather than a deliberately interleaved learning experience.

The strongest architecture is a guided recognition–explanation–application spiral:

  1. begin with an ordinary moment people recognise;
  2. let them notice or generate something safely;
  3. explain only what helps them understand that experience;
  4. show one neutral worked example;
  5. retrieve the idea through more than one participation mode;
  6. use it privately; and
  7. return later with greater realism and less support.

This is an evolutionary optimisation, not a parallel workshop. It preserves Hunter's decision that the meaning must not be stripped out, while correcting the current package's longest stretches of explanation and school-like retrieval.

Status and authority

  • Artifact reviewed: the complete current proposition: 80-screen deck, facilitator guide, participant materials, operational package, governing decisions and existing research—not the deck in isolation.
  • Current stage: revised internal candidate.
  • Not claimed: Hunter approval, participant validation, independent cold-founder review, qualified accessibility/safeguarding/privacy approval, facilitator proof or delivery readiness.
  • Execution condition: these are role-based lenses produced in one accountable AI context from the governed packs. They are inspectable synthesis, not bounded specialist reviews, 20 independent human experts or 20 separately trained models. Compass's required cold read cannot validly run in this same context because the reviewer has seen the builder rationale; that gate remains open.

Sources and equipment used

The producing context had loaded the 2026-08-13 specialist knowledge index, readable packs, shared MFC onboarding orientation, D-0010, D-0015, D-0016, D-0091, D-0094, D-0100, Stage 8 learning/transfer/context/safety/measurement syntheses, founder/Gina language sources, market/competitor work and the current unified package. Because individual call records were not preserved, this report does not claim that every role independently reviewed every named source. Baseline packs are starting toolkits, not professional accreditation.

Architecture comparison

Candidate What the panel found Decision
A. Education-led Strong on meaning and framework integrity; weakest on attention, energy and delay before meaningful use. Narrow, do not discard.
B. Experience first Strong on relevance; too risky if experience is unguided, personal or treated as broad productive failure. Reject as the whole architecture.
C. Recognition–experience–explanation spiral Best balance of meaning, dignity, retrieval, application and room energy when experiences are bounded and facilitator-supplied. Adopt as the organising architecture.
Hybrid A+C Keeps the three blocks and full conceptual spine, but converts long explanation/drill sequences into guided cycles. Recommended implementation.

The evidence supports principles—segmentation, signalling, worked examples, explanatory feedback, retrieval and varied practice. It does not scientifically specify a slide count, exact minute ratio or perfect workshop sequence. The recommendation is a reasoned product judgement constrained by that evidence and MFC's approved intent.

Specialist findings

Purpose, outside world and mission

Role Position and strongest objection Evidence strength and limit Recommendation / what would change it
Scout — market and ecosystem MFC should learn from RULER's implementation architecture—adult modelling, visible tools and repeated use—not copy its branded classroom tools. Strongest objection: the workshop still risks being a memorable event without an implementation environment. Comparator evidence is useful but largely developer-led, school-based and not direct evidence for Australian adults. Keep visible take-home objects and name the host/continuation layer separately. Change view if adult MFC pilot evidence shows the workshop alone produces reliable later retrieval.
Sasha — category strategy The distinctive proposition is accessible capability-building and integrated moment-based practice, not invention of every mechanism. Strongest objection: too many internal terms can make the category harder rather than clearer. Strong MFC positioning evidence; weak direct market proof that buyers or participants understand the category this way. A participant should be able to explain mental fitness without reciting HOS or all five skills. Change view after tested participant explanations show the current terminology improves clarity.
Ronan — public health and systems Individual practice is legitimate only when structural and relational constraints stay visible. Strongest objection: shared/team activities can imply people should skill their way through unsafe work, workload or missing support. Strong principle and authoritative workplace-health context; no MFC population-impact evidence. Preserve explicit system/support boundaries and keep shared Radar conditional. Do not claim prevention or social change from one session.
Grace — impact and theory of change The credible pathway is teaching → comprehension/retrieval → first attempted use → learning. Strongest objection: the workshop gestures toward wider ripples without a measured causal bridge. Coherent internal theory and general mechanism evidence; no direct MFC outcome evidence. Trace every major beat to a proximal outcome and decision signal. Treat movement effects as hypotheses. Change view only with observed longitudinal implementation evidence.
Iris — audience and culture Recognition, privacy and ordinary language are strengths. Strongest objection: spoken group response, rapid choral recall and shared writing may privilege confident, fast, English-fluent participants. Strong inclusion rationale; no current varied-participant comprehension evidence. Provide silent, card/gesture and spoken routes; test with varied intended adults. Internal persona reasoning cannot clear this.
Noa — strategy Optimise the flagship enough to learn from a real pilot; do not perfect every future layer first. Strongest objection: adding more concepts or a second product is an attractive distraction. Strong fit with current strategy and actual constraints; buyer value remains untested. Keep the three-block flagship, remove avoidable burden, freeze one research candidate and test it. Stop expanding scope until the first delivery evidence exists.
Talia — source integration Newer polish must not override approved decisions. Strongest objection: the current Radar worksheet drifted from Hunter's recorded three-moment decision into up to six moments. Direct conflict between D-0010 and the former current artifacts; high confidence. Restored exactly three moments total and one possible next move for each; opt-out remains without silently changing the product structure.

Learning, behaviour and participant experience

Role Position and strongest objection Evidence strength and limit Recommendation / what would change it
Reed — learning design Adopt the A+C hybrid spiral. Strongest objection: ten near-consecutive traffic-light recall prompts emphasised mapping and compliance more than meaning or flexible use. Retrieval, worked examples and explanatory feedback are well-supported general principles; exact MFC form remains untested. Replaced part of the drill with one neutral worked scenario, then retrieval in multiple modes. Kept the three corrections and later private practice.
Milo — behavioural/social context The design properly rejects intention as behaviour, but host conditions remain underdeveloped. Strongest objection: cueing one moment may be infeasible where power, workload or safety remove opportunity. Strong general behaviour/context evidence; no MFC real-world use data. Ask what makes the move easier or harder; preserve support/boundary/system-change options and no-opportunity measurement.
Remy — habit, identity and practice The low-stakes rep, cue and lapse-normalisation are directionally strong. Strongest objection: “most people's first attempt fades” was an unsupported population claim. Mechanism evidence supports cueing/repetition broadly; no MFC habit or maintenance evidence. Replaced the claim with possible barriers and lapse language; return remains normal without streak or blame.
Wren — experience/UX One projected job per screen is defensible, but screen count is not room quality. Strongest objection: facilitator, projection, cards, displays and private worksheets create heavy attention switching. Strong design rationale; no room observation. Use slides only where the room needs a shared visual; put stable reference material on cards; observe switching during rehearsal. Do not target a smaller number for its own sake.
Nova — messaging The human premise and “gap in what we were taught, not a gap in you” are strong. Strongest objection: absolute lines such as “Thoughts aren't facts” and dense coined nouns can sound reductive or clinical. Strong founder/Gina language record; exact participant response untested. Replaced it with “Not every thought is a fact”; read every load-bearing line aloud; explain MFC terms through ordinary moments.
Indigo — creative direction The colour/shape/word redundancy is useful. Strongest objection: the deck is a functional text presentation, not yet a designed emotional room journey. Internal visual specification and render checks only; no professional creative or projection approval. Design transitions, silence, artifacts and facilitator presence as part of the medium. Rehearsal and real-distance projection decide combining/adding screens.
Cole — delivery design The guide has unusually strong recovery and boundary detail. Strongest objection: the package still depends on unbuilt assets, conditional routes and a facilitator carrying too many simultaneous controls. Strong operational analysis; no timed room evidence. Rehearse with actual materials; log missed scripts, transitions and recovery. Remove or simplify any control the facilitator repeatedly misses.
Kai — participation Private-by-default is the right floor. Strongest objection: shared butcher paper and live collective agreement can create compliance through visibility and social pressure. Strong design/safety rationale; no actual cohort evidence. The private route is now the routine floor. Shared writing/team Radar require a separately approved module and “no shared route” remains complete.
Piper — measurement The D-0100 lean core is aligned to the workshop's honest proximal outcomes. Strongest objection: four minutes for Form 2 is still an estimate and may create end-of-session pressure or incomplete data. Strong construct/timing discipline; exact item comprehension and burden are untested. Protect a tested completion window outside teaching; predefine what result changes what workshop decision; preserve voluntary completion and paper/digital parity.
Quinn — experimentation Architecture, comprehension, retrieval, facilitator load and real-world use are separate uncertainties. Strongest objection: “pilot the workshop” is too vague to learn efficiently. Strong experimental logic; no completed test. Predefine architecture walkthrough, room rehearsal, question comprehension, participant usability and later opportunity/use tests. Do not let satisfaction decide architecture.

Boundaries, integration and founder gate

Role Position and strongest objection Evidence strength and limit Recommendation / what would change it
Ash — restricted accessibility/safeguarding screen Choice and privacy language are strong, but T4/T5/T6/T7 fire. Strongest objection: support wording, workplace power, shared writing, data routes and cohort access are unresolved. Direct artifact screen against the unreviewed T1–T8 set; not qualified-human assurance. Keep participant delivery blocked. Route clinical/support, privacy/legal, host, insurer and accessibility matters to the named humans.
Relay — reconciliation The advice converges on targeted optimisation, not rebuild or acceptance-as-is. Strongest objection: findings have historically been logged without changing the artifact. High confidence in the recorded conflict and change trace; effectiveness remains untested. Accepted the Radar, retrieval, language and participation corrections; preserved human gates and testing uncertainties; projections must now regenerate.
Compass — founder trace audit only The recommendation and “why” are visible. Strongest objection: Hunter still has not seen a rendered revised build, and this context cannot validly conduct its own cold read. Strong direct founder-source trace; cold-reader independence absent. Do not call this a Compass pass. Run a fresh-context cold read after the revised build, then show Hunter the artifact and rationale.

Reconciliation decisions

Accepted and implemented

  1. Restored the Radar to exactly three personally meaningful moments total, with one possible next move for each; one chosen cue may support one priority moment.
  2. Replaced the most mechanical part of the traffic-light drill with a neutral worked example and multimodal retrieval while retaining reconstruction and the three corrections.
  3. Replaced absolute or unsupported claims: “Thoughts aren't facts” and “most people's first attempt fades.”
  4. Made private participation the routine floor; shared writing and team Radar remain separately gated modules.
  5. Named the architecture as the A+C guided spiral and preserved the reasoning here.

Accepted as testing requirements, not implemented claims

  • actual room flow, cognitive load, projection and facilitator recovery;
  • participant comprehension, dignity, accessibility and findability;
  • exact Form 2 burden and question comprehension;
  • initial real-world opportunity and attempted use; and
  • whether exactly three Radar moments feel manageable and useful.

Preserved boundaries

  • D-0016's six original matters remain unresolved; the digital follow-up exposure remains open.
  • AI screening does not satisfy clinical, legal, privacy, safeguarding, insurance or accessibility approval.
  • The workshop cannot claim habit, prevention, wellbeing improvement, competence or organisational change.
  • The shared/team route is not the routine D-0100 measurement pathway.

Rejected or deferred

  • Rebuild the entire workshop as an unguided experience-first format — rejected as unnecessarily risky and inconsistent with Hunter's meaning-first correction.
  • Reduce the deck to a target number — rejected; the count follows room and learning jobs.
  • Add more theories, tools or a deeper second product before the first pilot — deferred.
  • Treat this same-context role panel as independent professional or founder assurance — rejected.

Quality decision

PARTIAL DESIGN-INTELLIGENCE RESULT — internal Hunter viewing is appropriate; specialist contract not yet proven. The Radar conflict, retrieval design, unsupported language and participation default have been corrected in the current internal package. The package may be shown to Hunter for visibility and direction. Before the system claims a completed design-intelligence review, the most decision-bearing lenses must be rerun through saved bounded task packets and unique contract-complete outputs, followed by reconciliation and learning return. A genuinely fresh-context founder/mission read and timed rehearsal also remain open. Participant delivery remains stopped.

Next decision gate

Hunter should be shown the revised rendered build, the participant journey and this rationale now, without describing it as final or fully panel-reviewed. His reactions can shape the next bounded review questions. A later approval request should follow the contract-complete specialist test and fresh-context founder read. Approval still would not clear delivery; qualified-human, production, rehearsal and participant-testing gates remain.

13 Contrast Asset Spec And Readability Pass

Contrast activity asset specification, and plain-language readability pass

Two deliverables in one file.

Deliverable 1 turns Beat 13's contrast activity (1:51–2:15) from a description into something a producer or a facilitator can actually execute. Until now it existed as one sentence — "a scenario run without the skill, then the same scenario with it" — in the design of record (01-three-hour-design.md:93), the facilitator guide (10-facilitator-guide-3hour.md:833) and the storyboard (11-participant-materials-and-storyboard.md, Beat 13). It is named in all three as the highest-leverage stretch in the session and it is the only one of the eighteen beats that cannot be delivered from the documents that exist. This closes that.

Deliverable 2 is the plain-language readability pass on all ten participant materials in 11-participant-materials-and-storyboard.md. That document's own accessibility specification lists "No plain-language readability check has been run on the copy above. Required before print" as the first item in §10 What this specification does not deliver, and again in its open-gates table. This performs that pass, with measured figures rather than asserted ones — and then states honestly what a pass of this kind still cannot close.

What this is not. Approved. Pilot-ready. Safe to deliver. Nothing here touches D-0016, which stands at 0 of 7. Nothing here authorises participant-facing delivery, and Deliverable 2 explicitly cannot close the readability gate on Material 10 — see §2.14.

DELIVERABLE 1 — The contrast activity, production-ready

1.0 What this asset has to do, and the constraints it is built inside

The beat's job is stated in the design and is narrow: the gap is felt rather than described. Everything else in the session describes Stop–Shift–Do. This is the only place a participant watches it happen at real speed, in a moment they recognise, and forms their own read of the difference before anyone tells them what the difference was.

Binding constraints, carried from the governing records and not negotiable here:

Constraint Source
Same situation shown twice; the debrief question is what did you notice, not what was right 11, Beat 13 (E)
Context-neutral; no clinical content, no distress, no crisis 11, Beat 13 (E); D-0005; K-08 rules 1–3
Not distressing, not bereavement, not illness, not conflict escalation, nothing plausibly someone's live situation 10, 1:53–2:07
The Do is not the perfect action; the outcome does not decide whether it counted K-07; Mental Rep locked outcome-independence
Shift is not always calming down, and may be skipped K-07; K-08 rule 9; D-0054
Stop is not freezing K-07; D-0054; Hunter's own instruction
No implication that struggle or difficulty accessing skills is a personal failure K-08 rule 3
Captions and a transcript mandatory on any film or audio; no uncaptioned media 11, Beat 13 and Accessibility §5
No causal, guarantee, treatment or outcome language K-08; 11 claims sweep
No stock photography of distressed people, anywhere, ever 11, standing slide rules
Scenario content and medium are flexible (D-0014); the function is essential 10 §1.3

Because scenario content is flexible, this specification is a strong default, not a new essential element. A facilitator may substitute — within the constraints above and §1.5's prohibitions. Nothing in this file creates a new D-0014 essential element, and no decision record is required to use a different scenario.

1.1 Timing — the fourteen minutes, allocated

01 and 10 both allocate 1:53–2:07 to the contrast and 2:07–2:15 to the pair debrief. Within the fourteen minutes:

Clock Duration What happens
1:53:00 0:30 Facilitator framing. "Watch this. You're not judging it and there's no right answer to spot. Just watch."
1:53:30 2:40 Version 1 — without
1:56:10 0:30 Reset. "Same moment. Again." Nothing else said.
1:56:40 3:10 Version 2 — with
1:59:50 5:40 Whole-room: "Don't tell me what they did right. Tell me what you noticed was different." Three or four contributions from volunteers.
2:05:30 1:30 Transition to pairs; buffer
2:07:00 Pair debrief begins (§1.6)

Total film runtime, both versions: 5:50. The two versions must sit within 30 seconds of each other, and the difference must come from the pause itself, not from added dialogue. A "with" version that is a minute longer teaches that using the skill takes a minute. It does not.

1.2 Scenario A — "The kettle" (primary)

1.2.1 Why this situation

It is the end of an ordinary day, in an ordinary kitchen, over an ordinary undone task. There is no crisis, no conflict, no workplace, no illness, no third party at risk. The pressure is real but small: accumulated tiredness meeting a reasonable question at the wrong second. Most adults have been both people in it.

Critically, the person who is asked the question has done nothing wrong and is played with complete neutrality. There is no antagonist. If the room can locate a villain, the scenario has failed (§1.7).

1.2.2 Characters
Sam The person whose moment this is. Gender not specified. Age not specified.
Jules The other person in the kitchen. Two lines. Gender not specified.

Casting and framing notes, binding:

  • The relationship between Sam and Jules is never named and must not be inferable. No wedding rings, no shared-bedroom cues, no photographs on the fridge, no pet names, no "love"/"mate"/"hon". They live in the same place. That is the entire specification. A viewer will supply partner, sibling, housemate, adult child, parent, friend — and every one of those readings works.
  • No children present, referenced, or audible. Not because children are unsuitable, but because a child in frame instantly narrows the scenario to parents and adds a caretaking obligation that changes what the "without" version means.
  • Cast Sam and Jules to reflect the room MFC is actually delivering to. Neither is written with any ethnicity, accent, class or body implied. Two performers of the same or different apparent age both work.
  • Sam is not a caricature of a stressed person. No dishevelment, no sighing, no hand through hair, no bag dropped heavily. Sam is fine. That is the point. The tiredness is legible in tempo, not in performance.

1.2.3 VERSION 1 — WITHOUT

INT. KITCHEN — EARLY EVENING

Sam comes in. Bag down on a chair. Coat still on. Fills the kettle at the tap, sets it on its base. Not hurried. Not slumped. The tempo of someone at the end of a long, unremarkable day.

Jules is already in the kitchen, rinsing a mug. Not waiting for Sam. Barely looks up.

JULES Oh — did you send that form back?

Sam's hand goes to the kettle switch. Presses it. Does not turn round.

SAM No.

A beat. Still not turning round.

SAM (CONT'D) I've had a day.

Flat. Not shouted. Not cold enough to be a row. Just closed.

JULES Okay.

Jules takes the mug and goes. Not offended, not slamming anything — just gone.

Sam stands at the counter. The kettle starts to build. Sam takes out their phone and looks at it. Knows exactly what just happened. Does nothing about it.

Hold. Cut.

Running time 2:40. Approximately half of that is Sam arriving and filling the kettle before Jules speaks — this is deliberate, it establishes the tempo, and it must be identical in Version 2.

What makes this sympathetic rather than contemptible: Sam does not snap, insult, or escalate. Sam gives a short flat answer while facing away, which is the most common thing in the world. The camera does not judge it, no music comments on it, and Sam's final look at the phone is recognition, not stupidity. A viewer's honest response should be yeah, I've done that, not what an idiot.

1.2.4 VERSION 2 — WITH

INT. KITCHEN — EARLY EVENING

Identical. Same coat, same bag, same chair, same tap, same tempo.

JULES Oh — did you send that form back?

Sam's hand goes to the kettle switch —

— and stops. Does not press it.

(THE STOP. See §1.4 for how this is shot. Roughly two and a half seconds. Sam does not close their eyes, does not breathe theatrically, does not look up and away. The hand simply does not complete the movement.)

Sam takes their hand off the switch. One out-breath — ordinary, the kind you don't notice yourself doing. Turns round and faces Jules.

SAM No, I didn't. Sorry — I'm not annoyed at you, I'm just fried. Can I do it after dinner?

JULES Sure.

A small pause. It is still slightly awkward.

JULES (CONT'D) There's pasta left.

Jules takes the mug and goes.

Sam stands at the counter. Presses the kettle. Takes out their phone and looks at it.

Hold. Cut.

Running time 3:10.

The last shot is identical to Version 1 — same framing, same duration, same phone. Nothing has been rescued. Sam is still tired, still on their phone, and the form still is not sent. That identical closing shot is the single most important craft decision in the asset, because it is what stops the piece from teaching use the skill and the evening gets better.

Dialogue alternates, if "fried" will not land in the delivery region or with an EAL-heavy room — substitute one of: "I'm just wiped", "I've got nothing left today", "I'm just done in." Do not substitute anything that names an emotion as a label ("I'm feeling overwhelmed") — that is emotional labelling, which K-08 rule 8 and K-06 push against, and it makes Sam sound like they have been on the course.

1.2.5 The difference audit — proof that only the skill changed

Everything in the left column is identical, frame for frame where filmed:

Held constant
Location, dressing, props, time of day, lighting, lens, camera position Identical setups
Both performers, wardrobe, hair Identical
Sam's arrival, bag, coat, filling the kettle Identical, same duration
Jules's line, tone, and delivery Identical take where possible
Jules's exit with the mug Identical
Sam's final action and final shot Identical, same duration
Music None, in either version
Narration, voiceover, on-screen text None, in either version

Permitted differences — exactly four, and each is the skill:

# Difference What it is
1 Sam's hand stops on the switch; ~2.5s before answering Stop — catching the moment
2 Hand off the switch, one out-breath, turns to face Jules (~3s) Shift — creating enough space; body and orientation. Visibly not calming down, and it takes three seconds
3 Sam's reply: 16 words instead of 5, facing Jules, naming the state and making a request Do — the next move with intention
4 Jules adds "There's pasta left" A consequence of 1–3, not a change to the setup

Plus two craft asymmetries, both of which exist solely to make difference 1 visible, and both of which are declared in §1.4 rather than smuggled in: the ambient-sound drop, and the unbroken shot across the pause.

If anything else differs, the contrast proves nothing and the debrief will produce noticings about lighting, mood or acting rather than about the moment.

1.3 Scenario B — "The cancellation" (alternate)

Provided because Scenario A assumes Sam lives with someone. Single-person households are a large minority in both the UK and Australia (no figure is asserted here — this is a design assumption, not a cited statistic), and in some delivery contexts — older-adult groups, community groups, mixed open-enrolment rooms — a kitchen shared with another adult is not a neutral image. Scenario B requires one performer and one prop, which also makes it the easier live role-play.

EXT./INT. BUS — LATE AFTERNOON

Sam is on a bus, coat on, bag on knees, halfway across town. Phone in hand. Looking out of the window.

The phone buzzes. A message from a friend: "I'm so sorry — I'm going to have to bail on today. Rain check?" It is the second time.

WITHOUT (2:40). Sam reads it. Jaw sets, barely. Types with one thumb: "fine." Sends it. Turns the phone face down on their knee. Looks out of the window. The bus keeps going. Sam does not get off. Hold. Cut.

WITH (3:10). Identical up to the message. Sam reads it. The thumb goes to the keyboard — and stops. (THE STOP: ~2.5s, thumb hovering, the typing indicator not appearing.) Sam looks up and out of the window for two seconds — not a technique, just off the screen. (The Shift: attention.) Then deletes what was there and types: "Ah, that's a shame. Next week?" Sends it. Turns the phone face down on their knee. Looks out of the window. The bus keeps going. Sam does not get off. Hold. Cut.

Identical closing shot again, and this one is even blunter: Sam is still halfway across town for nothing, still disappointed, still on a bus. The only thing that changed is what got sent.

Known adjacency, disclosed: Material 6's worked example is also a message-avoidance scenario. It is issued at 3:03, an hour after this beat, and is structurally different (days of not replying versus sixty seconds after a cancellation). Scenario A avoids the adjacency entirely and is the default for that reason; use B where a shared household cannot be assumed.

1.4 Route 1 — FILM

1.4.1 The hard problem: how to film a pause

A Stop is two seconds of nothing happening. Filmed naïvely it reads as an actor forgetting a line. Filmed conventionally — slow motion, a music sting, a rack focus, a heartbeat on the soundtrack — it reads as melodrama, and worse, it depicts time stopping, which teaches the exact misreading D-0054 exists to prevent: Stop is not freezing.

Five techniques, all cheap, all required:

  1. Give the pause a physical action to live inside. Sam's hand goes to the switch and does not press it. The pause becomes an interrupted movement, not an absence of movement. The viewer's eye has somewhere to be. This is the whole solve; everything below supports it.
  2. Hold one unbroken shot across the pause. Version 1's reactive beat is cut at roughly two- second intervals — propulsive, no room in it. Version 2 holds a single shot from Jules's line through Sam's reply, ~9 seconds unbroken. The edit rate is the teaching. Nobody in the room will be able to articulate this, and every one of them will feel it.
  3. Drop the room tone under the pause. For ~2 seconds the kettle hum, the tap drip and the street outside come down 8–10 dB and Sam's own out-breath comes up. Restore on the reply. This is the most effective available rendering of an interior pause and it costs nothing in post. Accessibility condition, binding: because this is an audio-only cue it must be duplicated in the captions ([room noise fades] / [room noise returns]) and in the transcript, and the shot must hold long enough that a deaf viewer reading the caption still sees the held hand.
  4. Shoot Sam's hand and Sam's face in the same frame. A cutaway to the hand tells the viewer where to look, which is the job the debrief is supposed to do. A medium shot that contains both lets each viewer notice whichever one they notice — which is what the prompt then asks about.
  5. Let Version 2 be slightly awkward. The pause should be a beat too long for comfort. Real ones are.

Prohibited entirely: slow motion; freeze frame; ripple, blur, or desaturation effects; heartbeat or breath sound design beyond the natural out-breath; any music in either version; voiceover of Sam's thoughts; on-screen text of any kind, and in particular any STOP / SHIFT / DO caption over the action. The on-screen labels are the most tempting and the most damaging: they convert an observation task into a comprehension check and pre-empt the entire debrief.

1.4.2 Shot list — Version 1 (WITHOUT), 2:40

# Shot Dur. Content Audio
1 WS kitchen, static, locked off 0:20 Empty kitchen. Jules at the sink, rinsing a mug, back three-quarters to camera. Room tone, tap
2 MS door / hallway 0:15 Sam enters, coat on, bag down on the chair. Door, bag
3 MS Sam at tap, profile 0:35 Fills the kettle. Unhurried. Sets it on the base. Water, kettle base click
4 Two-shot, Sam foreground / Jules background 0:12 Jules, still rinsing, barely looking up: "Oh — did you send that form back?" Dialogue
5 MS Sam, from behind and slightly to the side 0:08 Hand to switch. Presses it. Does not turn. "No." Beat. "I've had a day." Kettle begins
6 MS Jules 0:06 "Okay." Nothing on the face. Picks up the mug. Dialogue
7 WS, same as shot 1 0:10 Jules leaves frame. Sam still facing the counter. Footsteps, door
8 MS Sam, counter, static 0:44 Kettle builds. Sam takes out the phone. Looks at it. Recognition, held. Kettle rising, then click off
9 Hold on 8 0:10 No movement. Cut to black, no fade. Kettle silent

(Shot 8's length is what makes the ending land. Resist trimming it. It should be a little too long.)

1.4.3 Shot list — Version 2 (WITH), 3:10

Shots 1–4 are the same takes, cut identically — not reshot, not re-performed. Same file.

# Shot Dur. Content Audio
1–4 Identical to Version 1 1:22 Arrival, kettle, Jules's line. Identical
5 MS Sam, containing hand and face, unbroken 0:32 Hand to switch — stops. Does not press. ~2.5s held. Hand comes off the switch. One out-breath. Sam turns to face Jules. "No, I didn't. Sorry — I'm not annoyed at you, I'm just fried. Can I do it after dinner?" No cut anywhere in this shot. Room tone drops 8–10 dB at the stopped hand; breath up; restores on "No, I didn't."
6 MS Jules 0:12 "Sure." Small pause — genuinely awkward, not warm. "There's pasta left." Picks up the mug. Dialogue
7 WS, same as V1 shot 7 0:10 Jules leaves frame. Sam now facing into the room, not the counter. Footsteps, door
8 MS Sam, counter, static — same setup, same length as V1 shot 8 0:44 Sam turns back, presses the kettle. Takes out the phone. Looks at it. Kettle rising, then click off
9 Hold on 8 0:10 No movement. Cut to black, no fade. Kettle silent

Note the arithmetic: V1 = 0:20+0:15+0:35+0:12+0:08+0:06+0:10+0:44+0:10 = 2:40. V2 = 1:22+0:32+0:12+0:10+0:44+0:10 = 3:10. The entire difference between the two films is shot 5 (0:08 → 0:32) and shot 6 (0:06 → 0:12) — 30 seconds, all of it pause and consequence, and at the outer limit §1.1 permits. Nothing was added anywhere else.

1.4.4 Accessibility requirements — film

Owner: A-12 (Ash). All of the following are conditions of use, not enhancements.

Requirement Specification
Open captions Burned in, as the default projected master. Venue playback configuration is the single most common cause of an uncaptioned screening; burning them in removes the failure mode. A separate clean master plus .srt is supplied for the digital pack.
Caption quality Verbatim, not paraphrased. Speaker-identified. Non-speech information captioned — [kettle boiling], [room noise fades], [room noise returns], [Sam breathes out]. 1–2 lines, ≥ 20 characters/second reading rate not exceeded. Positioned so they never cover Sam's hand.
Transcript Full transcript of both versions, including action lines, in the digital and plain-text packs. A transcript containing only dialogue is useless here — the asset is 90% action.
Audio description Supplied as a separate described version, not mixed into the master. The AD script describes observable action only, never inner state. "Her hand goes to the kettle switch. It stops. She takes her hand away. She breathes out. She turns round." It must never say "she pauses to think", "she considers", "she calms herself" — that hands a blind participant the debrief answer the sighted room has to work out, and it asserts an interior state the film deliberately does not assert.
Photosensitivity No flashing, no strobing, nothing above 3 flashes/second. Not a risk in this content; stated because it is a standing rule.
Contrast and legibility Caption text ≥ 4.5:1 against its own background plate, checked against the projected image in the room, not on a laptop.
Volume The room-tone drop must not require the master volume to be raised. Mix so the dialogue is intelligible at a comfortable level with the drop applied.
Alternative If for any reason the film cannot be played with captions, the facilitator runs the live route instead. No uncaptioned media may be used (11, Accessibility §5).

1.4.5 What must NOT be depicted — film

  • Crying, shaking, hyperventilating, a raised voice, a slammed door, a thrown object.
  • Any escalation. Jules must not react. Jules's "Okay" is neutral, and if the performance carries even mild hurt, the room watches a relationship being damaged instead of a moment being missed.
  • Alcohol, cigarettes, medication, or any substance in frame.
  • Children, either present or referenced.
  • Any workplace, uniform, lanyard, laptop, or work call.
  • Anything that reads as a clinical setting, a therapy room, a waiting room, a helpline number, or a mental-health poster on a wall. Dress the kitchen and check the background.
  • A phone screen showing anything legible other than the message in Scenario B. No news, no social feed, no health app.
  • Sam appearing serene, wise, or improved in Version 2. Sam is exactly as tired in both.
  • Any suggestion Jules was owed the answer, or that Sam was in the wrong. The scenario has no fault in it.
  • Any depiction of the skill as effortful mastery — no visible technique, no counted breathing, no closed eyes. K-08 rule 6 bans forced breathwork and eye closure in the room; depicting them as the model is the same instruction one step removed.

1.5 Route 2 — LIVE ROLE-PLAY

This route is the default assumption for pilot, because MFC has no confirmed film budget and because a live run is materially more flexible. It is not a downgrade: in a room of twelve, a well-run live version is at least as strong as film, and the pause is easier to land live than on camera because the room's own silence does half the work.

1.5.1 Who plays whom — four stagings, in order of preference

Staging When Notes
1 Two facilitators. One plays Sam, one plays Jules. Any session with a co-facilitator. Strong default. Both rehearse. Jules's job is to be boring — same line, same tone, both times. The commonest live failure is a co-facilitator "helping" by playing Jules warmer in the second run, which destroys the difference audit.
2 One facilitator + one briefed non-participant. A host contact, a trainee facilitator, an MFC volunteer, briefed in advance. Single-facilitator sessions with a host relationship. A briefed non-participant is categorically different from a volunteer from the floor: they have seen the script, they have consented in advance, and they are not part of the group whose safety the session is promising.
3 Solo, "read-then-play". The facilitator stands outside a marked spot on the floor and reads the scene and Jules's line flatly from a card — "Jules is at the sink. Jules says: oh, did you send that form back?" — then steps into the spot and plays only Sam. Single facilitator, no second person, no volunteer. This is the standing fallback and it always works. This is a rehearsal-room convention (a staged reading), and rooms accept it without embarrassment because it is visibly not an attempt at drama. It also isolates the pause as the only performed content — which is exactly the only thing that needs performing. Do not attempt to play both characters in character. A single performer switching voices is a sketch, and the room will laugh.
4 Participant volunteer. Discouraged. See below.

1.5.2 On asking a participant to perform — the honest position

Do not build the activity on a participant volunteer. Four reasons, and the fourth is the governing one:

  1. They cannot be briefed, so they will improvise, and improvisation drifts toward drama.
  2. Whatever they improvise may be their own material. The scenario is designed to be recognisable; that is precisely why a participant performing it may not be performing.
  3. The room watches a peer be watched. Even a willing volunteer changes the room's sense of what might be asked of them next.
  4. It sits against D-0015. The session has promised, in writing on Material 1 and Material 10 and verbally at 0:00, that "you are never required to say anything personal out loud. Not once." A public request for a volunteer to act out a moment converts that promise into a promise with an implied exception. The cost of one good live moment is not worth the cost of the room re-reading the promise.

If a volunteer is used at all — and this should be rare — then all of the following, together: they play Jules only (two scripted lines, on a card, read not improvised); they are asked privately at the break, never publicly from the front; the ask includes an explicit, easy no ("say no and I'll do it differently, it makes no odds to me"); they never play Sam, and nobody is ever asked to play the person being answered flatly in Version 1.

1.5.3 If nobody volunteers

The design never reaches this state, because staging 3 requires nobody. That is the answer, and it is a design answer rather than a recovery answer.

Operationally: do not ask twice. Do not scan the room. Do not say "anyone? …no? …okay", do not say "come on", and do not fill the gap with a joke about the room being quiet. A second ask converts an invitation into pressure, and every participant present registers it. If an ask has been made and nothing comes back within about three seconds, the correct move is a flat, unbothered "Fine — I'll do it myself, it's easier anyway," and straight into staging 3.

1.5.4 Full live script

Staging. Mark one spot on the floor with tape or a chair before the session — the "kitchen". One real prop only: a mug, or a kettle if the venue has one. No coat, no bag, no set. The prop matters because it gives the hand something to stop on; without a prop, the pause has nowhere to live and the whole thing collapses into a facilitator standing still.

[SAY] — the framing, before Version 1

I'm going to show you something twice. Two and a half minutes each.

This isn't acting and it isn't a performance, so don't watch me — watch the moment. There's no right answer to spot and you're not judging it. Just watch.

[DO] Step into the spot. Do not look at the room again until both versions are finished.

VERSION 1 — WITHOUT

[DO] Mime filling the kettle. Take your time — this is where the tempo of a long day is established, and it is the part facilitators cut. Ten seconds of nothing but filling a kettle.

[JULES, or read from the card in staging 3]

Oh — did you send that form back?

[DO] Hand to the switch. Press it. Do not turn round.

[SAM]

No.

[DO] One beat. Still facing away.

[SAM]

I've had a day.

[JULES]

Okay.

[DO] Jules leaves — in staging 3, this is simply the facilitator saying nothing while the empty chair does the work. Sam stays at the counter. Take out a phone. Look at it. Hold for five full seconds. Then step out of the spot.

[SAY] — between versions. Four words. Nothing else.

Same moment. Again.

[DO] Do not say "now watch what's different", "this time with the skill", or "see if you can spot it." Every one of those tells the room what to notice and pre-empts the debrief.

VERSION 2 — WITH

[DO] Step back in. Identical mime, identical tempo. Do not shorten it because the room has already seen it.

[JULES]

Oh — did you send that form back?

[DO] The pause. This is the entire beat. Hand goes to the switch — and stops. Do not press it.

Count two full seconds in your head. Two seconds is much longer than it feels while you are doing it, and the untrained instinct is to cut it to nothing. This is the single most common failure of the live route. Rehearse it with a timer.

[DO] Take the hand off the switch. One ordinary out-breath — not a technique, not audible from the back, not performed. Turn round and face Jules.

[SAM]

No, I didn't. Sorry — I'm not annoyed at you, I'm just fried. Can I do it after dinner?

[JULES]

Sure.

[DO] A small awkward pause. Do not warm it up.

[JULES]

There's pasta left.

[DO] Jules leaves. Sam turns back, presses the kettle, takes out the phone, looks at it. Hold for the same five full seconds. Then step out of the spot — visibly, deliberately, one clear step — and only then look at the room.

1.5.5 How to run it without it becoming embarrassing theatre

Nine rules. Every one of them exists because breaking it is what makes a live demonstration cringe.

  1. Name it as a demonstration, not a performance. The framing line above does this. Rooms forgive a demonstration anything and forgive a performance nothing.
  2. Play it smaller than you think. Everything goes down: quieter than your facilitation voice, less movement, flatter. The instinct under mild embarrassment is to go bigger, and bigger is exactly what turns it into a sketch.
  3. No accents, no comedy, no exaggeration, no mugging. Jules is not a nag. Sam is not a grump.
  4. One real prop, no set, no costume. A coat and a bag are already costume.
  5. Never break the fourth wall mid-run. Do not look at the room, do not comment, do not react to a laugh. If the room laughs during Version 1, keep going — the laugh is recognition and it is fine.
  6. Physically de-role. Step into the spot to start, step out to finish. That single visible step is what tells the room the flat answer was not the facilitator's personality. Facilitators who skip it get read as having been genuinely short-tempered.
  7. If it goes wrong, do not rescue it with a joke. Say "let me run that again", flatly, and run it again. A joke tells the room the content was embarrassing, and by extension that their own version of this moment is embarrassing. That is the opposite of the session's whole frame.
  8. Rehearse the pause with a timer, out loud, three times, before the session. It is the only part of the entire facilitator guide that cannot be delivered cold.
  9. Do not narrate over either version. Already required at 10:1:53–2:07. Restated because the temptation is strongest in the live route, where the silence belongs to you.

Add to the rehearsal checklist (§11 of 10-facilitator-guide-3hour.md): "The two-second pause in the contrast activity, timed, three times."

1.6 The debrief — eight minutes, 2:07–2:15

1.6.1 The governing instruction

Participants are asked what they NOTICED, not what was correct. This is marked E in the storyboard and it is not a stylistic preference — it is the difference between a felt-gap activity and a comprehension check. A comprehension check at this point would teach the room that there is a right way to have watched, which retroactively converts the two versions into a worked example and destroys the only beat in the session where a participant forms their own read of the mechanism.

Corollary, binding on the facilitator: no noticing is confirmed, graded, corrected, or ranked. Not with words, not with "yes, exactly", not with a nod that is bigger for one answer than another.

1.6.2 Allocation

Clock Duration
2:07:00 0:30 Instruction and the "about the scenario, not yourselves" guard
2:07:30 6:00 Pairs, three questions
2:13:30 1:30 Two answers to question 3 pulled into the room; one-sentence link back; close

1.6.3 Exact prompts

[SAY] — the instruction

Pairs. Eight minutes. Whoever's next to you — and if you'd rather not, that's completely fine, sit with it on your own.

You're talking about the scenario, not about yourselves. Nothing personal is required here and nothing you say goes anywhere.

[DO] Put the three questions on screen, all three at once, and leave them up for the whole six minutes. Participants who lose the thread should be able to find it without asking.

1. Where exactly was the gap? Point at the second it happened, not the general feeling of it.

2. What did it cost them to take it? Because it cost something.

3. What would make that gap harder to find in real life?

[DO] Circulate. Do not sit down with a pair — a facilitator joining a pair makes that pair's conversation the assessed one. Six minutes.

1.6.4 Note on question 1

Question 1 presupposes there was a gap, and that is a deliberate, disclosed choice rather than an oversight. The open question has already been asked — the whole-room prompt at 1:59:50 is "tell me what you noticed was different", with no presupposition in it at all. Question 1 focuses the pair conversation after the open phase has run.

But the presupposition must not become a requirement. If a participant says "I didn't see one" or "there wasn't a gap", that is a legitimate answer and is welcomed, not corrected:

[SAY] Fair enough — where did you expect one to be? That's the more interesting question anyway.

1.6.5 Scripted responses to the four predictable answers

These are the four things rooms actually say. Each has one correct handling and at least one tempting wrong one.

The room says [SAY] Why
"They were calmer." "They were — although calmer isn't the target. What actually changed is that there was a gap. Calm is just what this particular gap happened to look like." K-08 rule 9; D-0054's amber correction. This is the highest-frequency answer and letting it stand teaches "Shift = calm down". Carried verbatim from 10.
"They did it right the second time." / "That's what you're supposed to do." "There isn't a right version. The second one isn't better behaviour — it's the same person with about three seconds of room in it. What did you actually see change?" The comprehension-check failure mode. Do not agree, and do not praise the observation.
"That's not realistic — nobody does that." "Probably right. Most of the time this person does version one. So does everyone in here. What we're looking at is one moment going differently, not a person being different." This is the single most valuable contribution the room can make and it must never be argued down. It is also the exact honesty of Material 6's closing paragraph. A facilitator who defends the scenario here has started selling.
"Nothing was different." "Okay — genuinely useful. Point at the second where you expected something and didn't get it." Accept it. Then use it.

One further handling, for the answer that carries risk. If anyone starts to describe their own version of this moment in the whole-room phase, the facilitator redirects immediately and warmly to the scenario — "I'll stop you there only because we're keeping this about them, not us — what did you notice in the second one?" The debrief is a D-0015 private-by-design beat (11, Accessibility §7) and the drift into personal disclosure is the failure it is designed against.

1.6.6 Closing the beat — 2:13:30

[DO] Pull two answers to question 3 into the room. They will name tiredness, other people watching, speed, and habit.

[SAY] — one sentence, then stop

Tiredness, people watching, speed, habit — that's Engine, Environment, and Pathways, from twenty minutes ago. That's all I'm going to say about that.

[DO] Do not re-teach the Human Operating System. The whole value of this moment is that the room produced the model's contents themselves without being asked to; explaining it back to them takes it off them. One sentence. Then the break.

1.7 What would make this asset fail

Named honestly, because each of these is a real and likely outcome of ordinary good intentions, not an exotic risk.

1. Melodrama. The most likely failure by a distance. It arrives through craft: a music cue under the pause, slow motion, a close-up on a trembling hand, a performer playing tired rather than being tired. It also arrives live, through a facilitator going bigger when they feel exposed. The symptom is that the room watches a story instead of a moment, and the noticings come back as "it was sad" rather than "there was a second where nothing happened." Countered by: no music in either version, identical treatment (§1.2.5), the prohibitions in §1.4.1, and live rule 2.

2. An implausibly serene "with" version. Sam becomes a person who has done the course. They breathe deliberately, speak warmly, and the evening improves. This teaches that the skill produces composure and good outcomes, which contradicts K-07 on three separate locks — Shift is not always calming down, Do is not the perfect action, and the mental rep's outcome-independence — and drifts straight into K-08's guaranteed-outcome territory. Countered by: the identical closing shot, the deliberately awkward pause after "Sure", the three-second Shift, and the "that's not realistic" handling in §1.6.5. Named contingency: if pilot feedback reads Version 2 as too resolved, the permitted trim is Jules's "There's pasta left" line. Cut it and Jules simply leaves.

3. A "without" version that invites laughing at the character. If Sam is written or played as oblivious, petulant, or stupid, the room gets to feel superior — and the session's entire non-shaming frame, built at 0:38 with "that's a gap in what we're taught, not a gap in you", collapses in one beat. It is worse than useless: a participant who laughs at Sam has been taught that the moment they recognise in themselves is contemptible. Countered by: Sam does not snap, Jules does not react, the flat answer is the most common thing in the world, and the closing shot is recognition rather than ignorance. Test: show Version 1 alone to someone outside the project. If their first response is anything other than a version of "yeah, I've done that", it fails.

4. A scenario that only lands for one demographic. Scenario A assumes a shared household; Scenario B assumes a phone and a friend. Neither is universal. A kitchen scenario in a room of people who live alone, or a bus scenario in a rural room where nobody uses public transport, produces polite blankness — which is indistinguishable from the activity working, because the whole beat is silent. Countered by: two scenarios with different assumptions; the deliberately unnamed relationship; no children, no workplace, no car, no named place; and the facilitator's D-0014 freedom to substitute. Not countered: F7 cross-cultural applicability remains open and unresolved, and this asset does not close it. A scenario built and reviewed inside one cultural frame is a mitigation, not a resolution.

5. Anything implying the skill guarantees a good outcome. The failure is rarely a sentence — it is usually structural: the "with" version ends better than the "without" version, and the room draws the obvious conclusion without anyone having claimed anything. This would be a K-08 breach delivered entirely through editing. Countered by: the identical final shot, identical final duration, and the fact that in both versions the form is still not sent, Sam is still tired, and Sam still ends up looking at their phone.

6. On-screen labels. Adding STOP / SHIFT / DO captions over the action, or a facilitator narrating "there's the Stop", is the single most tempting improvement anyone will propose. It converts the only observation task in the session into a labelling task, guarantees the debrief produces recall rather than noticing, and makes the eight-minute pair debrief redundant. This is prohibited in both routes.

7. Two versions that differ in more than the skill. Different lighting because the second was shot after lunch; a warmer Jules because the co-facilitator was being helpful; a longer "with" version because the actor found more in it. Each is invisible individually and each confounds the contrast. Countered by: the difference audit in §1.2.5, which should be checked against the final cut, not just against the script.

1.8 Reconciliation with the existing documents

Three items for the owners of files 01 and 10. None is blocking; all are one-line changes.

  1. 10-facilitator-guide-3hour.md, 1:53–2:07 currently offers three example scenarios, the first of which is "a short-notice request from a manager." This is not prohibited — K-07 carries a work context tag and the Radar uses it — but it is the weakest of the three for an open-enrolment room: it excludes anyone not currently employed, and it imports a power asymmetry that makes Version 1 read as the manager's fault rather than as a missed moment, which is exactly failure mode 3. Recommend demoting it and pointing the guide at this file's Scenario A.
  2. 01-three-hour-design.md:93 and 10:1:53–2:07 describe the contrast as 14 minutes of "contrast" with the debrief separate. This file's §1.1 allocates 5:40 of that 14 minutes to a whole-room noticing phase. That is consistent with 10's own script (which already takes "three or four contributions" inside the 14) and with the 44:56 ratio table, which counts all 14 minutes as participant-generated. No ratio change. No correction needed — recorded so the allocation is checkable rather than assumed.
  3. Rehearsal checklist (10 §11) gains one item: the timed two-second pause (§1.5.4).

DELIVERABLE 2 — Plain-language readability pass, all ten participant materials

2.0 Method, and what was actually measured

What was done. The participant-facing copy of each of the ten materials — the blockquoted text only, not the fidelity notes or design notes, which participants never see — was extracted programmatically and scored for Flesch–Kincaid Grade Level, Flesch Reading Ease, Gunning Fog, average sentence length, average syllables per word, and polysyllabic-word density. Every sentence over 20 words was listed and inspected individually. Em-dash and contraction density were counted separately. The whole corpus was then read line by line by A-08 (Nova) and A-12 (Ash) for the things formulae cannot see: idiom, ellipsis, register clash, jargon leakage, and constructions that are short and simple and still opaque.

Two figures are reported for each material, deliberately. Headings, table cells, form labels and write-in lines are not sentences, and including them inflates sentence length. Excluding them, however, hides real reading burden — Material 5's six-component table is the densest text on any participant material and a participant has to read it. Where the two figures differ materially, both are given.

Target. 11's own accessibility specification §1: "readable by an adult reading at roughly UK/AU school Year 6–8 level", average sentence length ≤ 15 words on cards and ≤ 20 on sheets, hard cap 25 words, zero clinical or clinical-adjacent vocabulary, minimal idiom, no abbreviations. Flesch–Kincaid grade 6–8 is the corresponding band.

Headline. The corpus is in good shape. Eight of ten materials sit at or below the Year 6–8 target, several comfortably below it. The two outliers are Material 5 and Material 10 — and Material 10 is the safeguarding card, which is the one place where reading difficulty carries a direct safety consequence rather than a comprehension one.

But the formula is the least interesting part of this pass. The best-scoring material in the corpus, Material 3 at grade 3.0, contains four idioms in eleven sentences and needs edits. Readability formulae reward short words and short sentences; "not enough in the tank" is four short words and is opaque to a large fraction of EAL readers. Every finding below that matters was found by reading, not by counting.

2.2 Locked wordings — the register of what this pass may not touch

Identified before editing, so that no rewrite below can accidentally cross one. Where a locked wording is genuinely hard to read, it is flagged as a kernel matter and left alone.

Locked wording Where Rewritable here?

Stop — catch the moment / Shift — create enough space where useful and available / Do — make the next move with intention (K-07) Material 4 front; Material 6 No
The mental rep definition, verbatim (K-07) Beat 14; echoed on Material 6 No

"The Passenger is not bad" (K-07) Material 5 No

Two locked wordings that are genuinely hard, flagged as kernel matters

Neither is rewritten here. Both are recorded so the kernel owners can see them.

  1. Shift — "create enough space to become workable — through your body, or through your thinking" (Material 2). Workable is being used as a predicative adjective applied to a state, not to a task — an unusual construction, and one that reads on first encounter as though the space becomes workable rather than the person. Material 3 explains "workable" thoroughly; Material 2, issued 54 minutes earlier at 0:47, does not. This is a sequencing problem as much as a wording one, and it has a non-kernel fix: see §2.4, edit M2-2.
  2. Focus — "put your attention where it matters and return it when it drifts" (Material 2). 15 words, two clauses, and "where it matters" is an abstract relative construction. It is the hardest of the five sentences to read and it is locked.

Kernel matter, for the record: if the five public skills' locked wordings are ever revisited by the committee, these two are the readability pressure points. K-07 is awaiting-committee in any case. This pass makes no recommendation to change them — a locked public wording is worth more than a grade level.

2.3 What was deliberately not simplified

11's accessibility spec asks for plain language. It does not ask for generic-wellness language, and the difference matters more here than the grade level does.

Kept exactly as written, and defended:

  • "a skill nobody sat you down and taught" (M1) — blunt on purpose. Any softening ("something many of us were never shown") removes the accusation and the accusation is the point.
  • "Workable is often nowhere near calm." (M3)
  • "You're not at a light. Nobody's holding you there." (M4)
  • "How it turns out does not decide whether it counted." (M4)
  • "That's not a character flaw. It's how people work." (M5)
  • "Most of the time, this person will still leave the message." (M6)
  • "This isn't a story about someone being fixed." (M6)
  • "that would just be a list of things you want other people to do differently" (M8)
  • "Most people's first attempts fade. That's expected, not failure." (M9)
  • "You don't restart. There's nothing to restart." (M9)
  • Every safeguarding, consent, privacy and opt-out line on M10. Clarity yes, reduction no — and every rewrite proposed for M10 in §2.12 makes the text longer, not shorter.

Also kept: the stacked negation in the three D-0054 corrections (M4 back) and in M5's "not a map of your brain, not a diagnosis, and not a description of what's wrong with you." 11's own spec already carves these out — "except in the three Stop–Shift–Do corrections, where the negation is the teaching" — and M5's triple negative is doing the same protective job under K-08 rules 2 and 3. Splitting it into two sentences is proposed; weakening it is not.

2.4 Material 1 — Workshop map · NEEDS EDIT (minor)

Grade 5.1 · Ease 79 · Fog 8.7 · avg 11.4 words · 3 sentences over 20 words · em-dash 3.4/100w (highest genuine prose density in the corpus).

This is the first thing a participant reads, often standing up, often before deciding whether to stay. It should be the easiest text in the pack and it is currently the fifth easiest.

M1-1 "Three hours of session across three and a half hours, with two 15-minute breaks — on a skill nobody sat you down and taught: handling the everyday moments your life is actually made of." (33 words; em-dash and colon in one sentence; the main clause is a noun phrase with no verb) The longest sentence in the pack, in the first paragraph of the first card. A low-literacy reader reaching the colon has lost the subject. "Three hours of session, across three and a half hours. Two 15-minute breaks.

It's about a skill nobody sat you down and taught you: handling the everyday moments your life is actually made of."

(Blunt line preserved word for word. Split into three sentences; longest is 20 words.)
M1-2 "Need something different — more time, a different seat, written instead of spoken? Tell a facilitator." Subject-dropped question ("[Do you] need…"). Subject-dropped interrogatives are a documented EAL barrier. "Do you need something different? More time, a different seat, written instead of spoken — just tell a facilitator. No explanation needed."
M1-3 "facilitator" — first use, and used again on M7, M8, M9, M10, never defined anywhere Four syllables, low everyday frequency, and a participant who does not know it cannot act on any of the five instructions that depend on it — including two safeguarding instructions on M10. On first use only: "tell a facilitator (one of the people running today)". Every later use then works. This is the highest-value single edit in the corpus for the effort involved.

(23 words, double em-dash parenthesis) Two nested asides before the main verb resolves. "Then we'll show you the same situation twice. Once without any of this, once with it. Then you tell us what you noticed."
M1-5 "You'll pick a few real moments from your own life, decide what you'd do differently in them, and choose one reminder to take home." (24 words, three coordinated verb phrases) Over the 20-word sheet guidance; three actions in one breath. "You'll pick a few real moments from your own life. You'll decide what you'd do differently in them. And you'll choose one reminder to take home."

2.5 Material 2 — Skills reference card · NEEDS EDIT (one line)

Grade 4.8 · Ease 75 · Fog 6.2 · avg 8.0 words · no sentence over 20 words.

Five of the ten sentences are locked and untouchable. The card is otherwise clean. One genuine stumble and one sequencing fix.

# Flagged Why Proposed rewrite
M2-1 "Naming them is what makes them practisable." Two problems in seven words. "Practisable" is a low-frequency word absent from most plain-English wordlists and is a spelling trap in both AU/UK and US conventions. And it is a cleft construction ("X is what makes Y"), which is grammatically heavier than it looks. "Giving them names is what makes them something you can practise." — or, plainer still: "Once they have names, you can practise them." Preferred: the second. It is 7 words, grade 3, and says the same thing.
M2-2 "create enough space to become workable — through your body, or through your thinking" — locked, not rewritten Workable is undefined at 0:47 and is not explained until Material 3 at 1:41 — 54 minutes later. Non-kernel fix: add one unlocked line beneath the five, on the card: "'Workable' means you've got enough room to choose. We'll come back to it." The locked sentence is untouched; the gap it leaves is closed.

Also noted: "These aren't five things to get good at by Friday" uses "by Friday" as an arbitrary-deadline idiom. It is mild, it is good voice, and it is comprehensible from context. Keep.

2.6 Material 3 — State Check card · NEEDS EDIT (idiom density)

Grade 3.0 · Ease 87 · Fog 5.1 — the easiest-scoring material in the corpus, and it needs four edits.

This is the clearest demonstration in this pass of why a formula is not a readability check. Eleven short sentences containing five idioms or metaphors, in the material that defines one of the session's three core constructs, on a card the participant is asked to use in their own head with no facilitator present.

11's own spec §1 says: "Idiom and metaphor: minimal. Idioms are a known barrier for participants with English as an additional language and for some autistic adults." This card does not meet its own rule.

The fix is not to delete the idioms — they are what makes the card feel like a person wrote it. The fix is to pair each with its plain gloss, which costs about eleven words in total.

# Flagged Why Proposed rewrite
M3-1 "Too wound up, too urgent, too much load, too reactive." "Wound up" is a phrasal idiom with no literal reading. "Load" used as a bare abstract noun. "Reactive" is clinical-adjacent and is exactly the register 11 §1 bans. "Too tense, too urgent, too much to carry, snapping too fast." — every term literal, the rhythm and the four-beat structure kept.
M3-2 "Flat, foggy, checked out, not enough in the tank." Four metaphors in a row and not one is literal. "Checked out" and "in the tank" are both opaque to EAL readers; "foggy" is comprehensible-ish; "flat" is idiomatic in AU/UK, less so elsewhere. "Flat, foggy, switched off, running on empty — not enough in you for what this needs." Better still, and preferred: "Flat. Foggy. Not really here. Not enough left in you for what this moment needs." Keeps the tone; the last clause makes the whole line self-glossing.
M3-3 "more going on than this moment can use" "Can use" applied to a moment is an unusual animate construction. Mild. "more going on in you than this moment needs"
M3-4 "There's no score. There's no good answer." "No good answer" is genuinely ambiguous — it reads as "there is no answer that is good" rather than the intended "no answer is better than another." "There's no score. No answer is better than another."

Locked wording untouched: the State Check question itself. No colours, no scale — confirmed absent; D-0054's boundary and K-08 rules 7–8 hold on this card.

Keep exactly: "Workable is often nowhere near calm." and "Nobody ever asks you for this answer. It's yours."

2.7 Material 4 — Stop–Shift–Do card · PASS with two edits

Grade 3.9 · Ease 81 · Fog 6.9 · no sentence over 20 words.

The card people keep, and the strongest-written material in the pack. Two items.

# Flagged Why Proposed rewrite
M4-1 "Sometimes it's the opposite — getting sharper, getting moving, getting connected." "Getting moving" is not idiomatic English (the pattern wants "getting going" or "getting yourself moving"), and the three-fold "getting X" parallel breaks on the second item. A reader stumbles on the rhythm, not the meaning. "Sometimes it's the opposite — getting sharper, getting going, getting other people involved." ("Getting connected" is also slightly opaque; "getting other people involved" is what it means.)
M4-2 "Stop, Shift, Do is a handle for using the five skills while life is happening." "Handle" is a metaphor (a thing to grip) used without being named as one. 11 §1: "Where a metaphor earns its place… it is explicitly named as a metaphor on the same page." This one is not. It is also the closing line of the whole card, so it is the last thing read. "Stop, Shift, Do is something to grab hold of when you need the five skills and life isn't waiting. It isn't a sixth skill, and it isn't the whole framework." (Alternative, if the shorter line is preferred: keep "handle" and add "— something to grab hold of" once.)

2.8 Material 5 — Human Operating System sheet · NEEDS EDIT (significant)

Grade 6.4 prose / 8.0 including the table · Ease 72 / 57 · Fog 10.3 / 11.0 · polysyllabic 13.2% / 16.4% · avg 12.7 words · 3 sentences over 20.

The second-hardest material in the pack, and the densest beat in the session — 11 minutes, six components, delivered immediately after a 15-minute break. The sheet already carries the right mitigation ("You are not expected to memorise this"), which is why this is an edit and not a rebuild.

2.8.1 The finding that matters most: the table contains banned vocabulary

11's own accessibility specification §1 states:

Zero clinical or clinical-adjacent vocabulary on any participant material. No "regulation", "dysregulation", "activation", "co-regulation" as a bare noun, "cognitive", "emotional literacy", "resilience", "mindset", "wellbeing journey".

Material 5's Engine row reads:

Your body state — energy, arousal, activation, fatigue, tension, stress, breath, hunger, sleep pressure, recovery.

"Activation" is explicitly on the banned list and is on the sheet. So is "arousal", which is not on the list but should be: outside a physiology context its dominant everyday sense is sexual, and it is printed on a handout given to twelve adults in a room. "Sleep pressure" is a technical term from sleep science that most readers will not have met.

Status of this wording. These descriptors come from K-07's HOS table, and Material 5's own fidelity note says "Six components in K-07's wording." But K-07 declares its locked public wordings explicitly — the five skills, Stop–Shift–Do, the mental rep, the State Check, the Radar prompt, and "the Passenger is not bad" are each marked as locked. The HOS component descriptors are not. They are kernel-sourced but not declared-locked, and K-08 rule 12 (plain language) applies to them.

This is a genuine conflict between two of the document's own rules and it needs a ruling, not a unilateral edit. Proposed resolution, in order:

  1. Preferred: rewrite the participant-facing descriptors in plain words, keep K-07's wording in the facilitator guide, and add one line to Material 5's fidelity note recording that the sheet carries a plain-language rendering of K-07's components rather than its exact vocabulary. This is the same treatment 11 §1 already applies to "co-regulation" → "Connection", so the precedent exists inside the document.
  2. Minimum, if any change is refused: delete "activation" and "arousal" only. Both are redundant — "energy", "tension" and "stress" already carry the meaning — and "activation" is a direct breach of the document's own §1.

Proposed plain-language table:

Component Current Proposed
Driver Your access to awareness, attention, pausing, choice, and the next move with intention. What you can reach right now: noticing, paying attention, pausing, choosing, and making your next move with intention.
Passenger Thoughts, emotions, urges, impulses, protective reactions, wants, needs, memories, interpretations. The Passenger is not bad. Thoughts, feelings, urges, the things you want and need, memories, and the way you read a situation. The Passenger is not bad. (locked line untouched)
Engine Your body state — energy, arousal, activation, fatigue, tension, stress, breath, hunger, sleep pressure, recovery. Your body: energy, tiredness, tension, stress, breathing, hunger, how well you slept, how much you've recovered.
Pathways The familiar routes, made easier by repetition. Learned patterns, habits, defaults. The familiar routes — the things you do without thinking, because you've done them before.
Navigation Values, care, intention, direction, responsibility. What matters to you. What matters to you: what you care about, what you're aiming at, what you feel responsible for.
Environment People, place, demands, culture, cues, support, friction. What's around you: people, place, what's being asked of you, what helps, what gets in the way.

(Nine polysyllabic words removed; the six components, their meanings and their order are unchanged; the locked Passenger line is verbatim.)
